SSRNGEXAPV28p 7379989 ★★★★★

Momentum Strategies in ETFs under Simple Operational Rules: Economic Value and Conditional Predictability

ETF 모멘텀은 운용 규칙을 씌워야 돈이 된다.

ETF momentum pays only when operational rules wrap it.

Nicolás Magner, Aliro Joel Sanhueza · Universidad Diego Portales and Universidad Diego Portales

  • 순수 모멘텀만으로는 패시브보다 못하다는 문제
  • 기술적 진입, 다기간 랭킹, 손절·익절 144종을 얹었다
  • 샤프 1.3 초과, 최대낙폭 -7%로 개선됐다
  • 알파는 신호가 아니라 꼬리위험 축소에서 나온다
방법
고전 횡단면 모멘텀에 기술적 진입 신호, 슈퍼카테고리 분산을 강제한 8종목 다기간 랭킹, 손절·익절 규칙 144종을 겹쳐 쌓았다.
데이터
미국 상장 투자가능 ETF 3,215종을 2001~2026년 1,289주 구간에서 검증했고 편도 20bp 거래비용을 전 단계에 물렸다.
시사점
모멘텀 랭킹 위에 격주 매수·주간 청산 점검과 동적 손절·익절을 얹어 낙폭을 줄이는 운용 계층으로 쓴다.
적용도 5/5
규칙과 리밸런싱 주기가 다 적혀 있고 ETF 가격은 누구나 구하므로 그대로 백테스트할 수 있다. 순수 모멘텀이 무가치하다는 반증도 더했다.
  • Pure ETF momentum loses to passive, so what fixes it?
  • Add technical entries, multi-horizon ranks, 144 exit rules
  • Sharpe rises above 1.3; max drawdown shrinks to -7%
  • Alpha comes from tail-risk cuts, not the signal
Method
Classic cross-sectional momentum plus technical entry filters, an eight-position multi-horizon rank with forced super-category diversification, and 144 dynamic stop-loss/take-profit exits under biweekly buys and weekly exit checks.
Data
3,215 investable U.S. ETFs over 2001-2026, 1,289 weeks, charging 20 bps per side at every stage.
Use
Bolt the exit-rule and diversification layer onto an existing momentum sleeve to cut drawdowns.
Score 5/5
Rules, universe and cadence are fully specified on public ETF prices, and it also refutes plain ETF momentum, whose Sharpe runs -0.17 to +0.22 with 69-82% drawdowns.
ETF momentumcross-sectional momentumstop-losstake-profittail risktransaction costs
ORIGINAL ABSTRACTThe relevant empirical question about momentum in exchange-traded funds (ETFs) is not whether it works, but whether simple operational rules can extract value from it. We show that pure momentum over a broad ETF universe creates no value: replicated across 3,215 investable U.S. ETFs, it delivers Sharpe ratios between −0.17 and +0.22 with drawdowns of 69% to 82%, systematically below passive investing. Yet three layers of rules available to any investor fully reverse that conclusion. We evaluate the 2001–2026 period (1,289 weeks) across the investable universe, charging a 20-basis-point transaction cost per side at every stage of the analysis. On top of replicating classic cross-sectional momentum, we add technical entry signals, a multi-horizon momentum ranking with mandatory diversification across super-categories within an eight-position portfolio, and an expanded family of 144 dynamic stop-loss and take-profit exit rules, all under an asymmetric rebalancing regime of biweekly purchases and weekly exit monitoring. The complete strategy delivers a Sharpe ratio above 1.3 and a maximum drawdown of −7%, beating passive investing by close to a full Sharpe point; the alpha concentrates in tail-risk reduction and is impaired only during the high-implied-volatility regime. The central implication for researchers and practitioners is that the value comes not from the technical signal but from the operational management layer that surrounds it.

The Tail Is the Only Signal: Flush Reversion in Equity Indices and Crypto Perpetual Futures

폭락 다음날 반등 효과는 대부분 집계 오류이고, 지수 -7% 이하만 살아남는다.

Almost all buy-the-dip reversion is a counting artifact; only index drops of 7%+ survive.

Alexandr Dashyan

  • 폭락 반등 백테스트가 같은 날짜를 중복 계산한다
  • 날짜 단위 집계, 중첩 임계값, 다중검정, 부트스트랩 보정
  • 지수 -7% 이하 50건만 다음날 평균 3.08% 수익
  • 암호화폐 무기한선물은 6년 내내 베타 차감 후 음수
방법
이벤트 스터디에 날짜 단위 집계와 familywise 보정, 짧은 블록 부트스트랩을 함께 적용한다.
데이터
미국 주가지수 4종의 76년치와 단일종목 28개 패널, 암호화폐 무기한선물 20종의 6년치를 쓴다.
시사점
지수 -7% 이하 폭락일 종가에 사서 다음날 청산하는 규칙만 남기되, 자본 배분은 극히 낮게 잡는다.
적용도 5/5
진입·청산 규칙과 임계값이 명확하고 지수 일봉만 있으면 되므로 데이터 확보가 사실상 무료다.
  • Event studies double-count one shock across instruments
  • Fix: date-level counting, nesting, familywise, bootstrap
  • Index drops ≤-7%: next day averages +3.08%, p=0.006
  • Crypto perps: net-of-beta edge negative every year
Method
One event definition plus four corrections: date clustering, nested thresholds, familywise p-values, short-block bootstrap.
Data
Four US equity indices over 76 years, a 28-name panel, and 20 crypto perpetual futures over six years.
Use
Buy the index at the close after a 7% or worse drop, exit next session, and size it as a rare overlay.
Score 5/5
Rules and thresholds are explicit and need only free daily index prices, so data availability is a non-issue.
mean reversionevent clusteringmultiple testingblock bootstrapcrypto perpetualstail risk
ORIGINAL ABSTRACTBuying an asset immediately after a large single day decline is one of the oldest ideas in short horizon trading, and it is easy to make it look profitable. This paper applies one event definition and one testing protocol to two asset classes, four US equity indices over seventy six years and, in results carried over from an earlier stage of the same research program, twenty cryptocurrency perpetual futures, and finds that almost all of the apparent effect is an artifact of how the events are counted. Large declines arrive on the same few calendar dates across instruments, so an event study that treats each instrument day as an independent observation is counting one market wide shock many times. In a panel of twenty eight single names, 1,361 declines at or below seven percent are only 791 distinct dates, and the pooled t statistic of 6.76 falls to 1.68 when each date is counted once. Three further corrections matter and are usually skipped: the depth thresholds that define such events are nested rather than independent, so a strong tail leaks into every shallower cut; testing several depths requires a familywise correction; and a stationary block bootstrap with a block length that is a large fraction of the sample is badly anti conservative, which in our own first pass manufactured a p value two orders of magnitude too small. After all four corrections, exactly one result survives in equities. Index declines at or below seven percent, 50 events on 25 dates clustering into 10 episodes since 1950, are followed by a mean next session return of 3.08 percent, with a familywise p value of 0.006 and a bootstrap interval from 1.34 to 4.84 percent. It is not crash window drift: the next session returns 3.08 percent while each of the following nine averages 0.01 percent, below the unconditional daily mean. It is implementable, since 83 percent of the move occurs after the opening print. Everything shallower is indistinguishable from zero, and the corresponding single name effect is absent. In crypto perpetuals the same mechanism fails completely, with an edge net of market beta that is negative in every regime and every year of a six year sample. The economics are the final constraint: an account trading the surviving tail signal deploys 0.05 percent of its capital time and beats Treasury bills by 0.44 points a year, which is a real effect that cannot carry a portfolio.

Sectoral Intramonth Momentum Cycle: Exploiting Turn-of-the-Month Patterns in Sector ETF Strategies

미국 섹터 ETF에서 월중 모멘텀 주기를 찾아 매매 일정으로 바꾼 연구다.

Quantpedia turns an intramonth momentum cycle in sector ETFs into a dated trade schedule.

Cyril Dujava

  • 달력 효과 연구가 개별 주식에만 머물렀다
  • 252일 모멘텀을 월중 특정 일자에만 태운다
  • 롱숏 연 5.99%, 샤프 0.55를 기록한다
  • 월 거래일 절반도 안 되게 투자한다
방법
252일 추세 순위로 섹터를 줄 세우고 월중 세 구간에서만 방향을 바꿔 잡는다.
데이터
SPDR 섹터 ETF 9종과 SPY를 1998년 12월부터 2026년 6월까지 검증한다.
시사점
월초 1일 추세, 2~3일 반전, 월말 10~5일 전 구간을 각각 독립 신호로 붙여 쓴다.
적용도 5/5
ETF 종가만 있으면 그대로 재현되고 진입·청산 일자까지 명시해 5점을 준다.
  • Calendar-anomaly work stopped at single stocks
  • 252-day momentum, traded only on set month days
  • Long-short returns 5.99% a year at 0.55 Sharpe
  • Market-neutral leg: 3.77% at 0.54 Sharpe
Method
Rank sectors on trailing 252-day momentum, then flip direction across three intramonth windows.
Data
Nine Select Sector SPDR ETFs plus SPY, December 1998 through June 2026.
Use
Run momentum long day 1, reverse days 2-3, add the T-10 to T-5 month-end leg as a separate sleeve.
Score 5/5
Scores 5: daily ETF closes are free and public, and the entry and exit days are spelled out.
intramonth momentum cycleturn-of-the-monthsector ETFscalendar anomalylong-shortmarket-neutral
ORIGINAL ABSTRACTWe document a persistent intramonth momentum cycle in U.S. sector ETFs that yields meaningful risk-adjusted returns when properly sequenced. Using the nine original Select Sector SPDR ETFs and SPY as the market benchmark from December 1998 through June 2026, we show that trailing 252-day sector momentum generates a positive spread on the first trading day of the month—and then sharply reverses on days two and three. A third, independent leg of the cycle emerges in the window from ten to five trading days before month-end, consistent with the intramonth momentum cycle recently documented at the single-stock level by Nathan, Suominen and Tasa (2026). Stitching the three legs together into a single composite strategy delivers 5.99% annualized return at a 0.55 Sharpe ratio for the long-short variant, and 3.77% at 0.54 for the market-neutral variant—all while being invested fewer than half the trading days each month. Our contribution is twofold: we extend the calendar-anomaly literature from individual equities to sector-level portfolios, and we provide practitioners with a transparent, low-turnover framework that translates these academic patterns into actionable trade schedules.

Another Moment for CAPM

코스큐니스를 쪼개니 분산-분산 상관만 값이 매겨졌다

Splitting coskewness shows only its variance-variance part is priced.

Dmitry Malakhov

  • 비가우시안 CAPM의 3차 위험은 실증에서 늘 약했다
  • 수익률 적률 전개로 코스큐니스를 상관 항들로 분해
  • 마이크로캡 제외 파마-맥베스 회귀에서 최저차 항만 유의
  • 베타와 분산-분산 상관을 묶은 전략이 연 9%
방법
수익률 적률 전개로 코스큐니스를 개별주-시장 적률 간 상관들의 합으로 분해한 뒤 파마-맥베스 회귀로 각 항의 가격을 따로 추정한다
데이터
마이크로캡을 뺀 개별주 횡단면 수익률이며 표본 구간은 초록에 없다
시사점
코스큐니스 대신 분산-분산 상관을 팩터로 뽑아 베타와 함께 롱숏 포트폴리오를 짜본다
적용도 4/5
일별 수익률만 있으면 적률과 상관을 직접 계산할 수 있어 데이터 확보는 쉽지만 리밸런싱 주기와 포트폴리오 구성 규칙은 직접 정해야 해서 4점이다
  • Coskewness is theoretically a systematic risk but empirically weak
  • A return-moment expansion breaks it into stock-market correlations
  • Fama-MacBeth on non-microcaps prices only the lowest-order term
  • Beta plus variance-variance correlation returns ~9% a year
Method
The author expands returns in moments, decomposes coskewness into correlations between stock and market moments, then prices each component separately.
Data
Cross-section of individual US-style stock returns excluding microcaps; the abstract gives no sample window.
Use
Build a variance-variance correlation factor from daily returns and pair it with beta in a long-short book.
Score 4/5
Score 4: daily returns are all you need to compute the moments, but rebalancing cadence and portfolio construction are left open.
coskewnessCAPMFama-MacBethhigher-moment riskvariance-variance correlationcross-sectional asset pricing
ORIGINAL ABSTRACTThe non-Gaussian CAPM states that beta and coskewness are the only two systematic risks: beta captures second-order risk, while coskewness captures third-order risk. However, the empirical performance of coskewness is known to be weak. Using a return-moment expansion, I decompose coskewness into a sum of correlations between stock and market moments. If investors care less about higher-order risks, these components should receive unequal prices. In Fama-MacBeth regressions of individual stocks excluding microcaps, only the lowest-order component, the variance-variance correlation, earns a significant premium; higher-order cross-moment correlations do not. Thus, third-order risk is priced, but in a more nuanced way. A strategy combining beta and the variance-variance correlation earns about 9% annually, unexplained by Fama-French factors.

Factor Time

낡은 재무제표로 만든 팩터를 매월 갱신분과 나눠 쓰면 가격결정이 개선된다

Split factors into a stale fundamental component and a monthly-refresh component to price returns better.

Boone Bowles, Adam V. Reed, Matthew C. Ringgenberg, Jake Thornock · Mays Business School at Texas A&M University, University of North Carolina Kenan-Flagler Business School, University of Utah - Department of Finance and Brigham Young University

  • 기존 팩터는 몇 달 전 재무제표로 1년에 한 번만 포트폴리오를 짠다
  • 매월 최신 연차 재무제표로 팩터를 새로 만들어 기존 팩터와 비교했다
  • 갱신 전후 수익률 차이를 별도 팩터로 넣자 가격결정이 크게 개선됐다
  • 이벤트 스터디 CAR 수천 건의 해석이 뒤집히고 상위 10% 펀드의 14.7%가 재분류됐다
방법
최신 연차 재무제표로 매월 팩터를 재구성하고, 낡은 팩터에 포트폴리오 재배정에 따른 수익률 변화분을 추가 팩터로 붙였다
데이터
미국 상장기업 재무제표와 수익률, 이벤트 스터디 CAR, 뮤추얼펀드 성과를 썼다. 구체적 검증 구간은 초록에 없다
시사점
팩터 벤치마크를 느린 성분과 빠른 성분으로 쪼개 알파 귀속과 펀드 선별에 쓰면 된다
적용도 4/5
Compustat 재무제표와 CRSP 수익률만 있으면 재현되지만 매매 규칙까지는 직접 설계해야 해서 4점이다
  • Standard factors rebalance annually on financial statements months old
  • Authors rebuild factors monthly from the latest annual statements
  • Fresh factors help a little; adding the update-induced return change helps a lot
  • Reverses thousands of event-study CARs, reclassifies 14.7% of top-decile funds
Method
Monthly factor reconstruction from the most recent annual statements, plus a second factor for the return change from reassigning stale portfolios.
Data
US firm financial statements and returns, event-study CARs, and mutual fund performance; the abstract gives no sample window.
Use
Use the two-component benchmark to attribute alpha and screen managers whose edge is just stale-factor drift.
Score 4/5
Score 4: reproducible from Compustat and CRSP, both standard, but entry/exit rules and universe are left to you.
factor modelsstale dataportfolio rebalancingevent study CARsmutual fund performanceinformation arrival
ORIGINAL ABSTRACTFactor models conventionally form portfolios annually using stale financial statements released months earlier. We construct fresh factors each month using the most recent annual financial statements. Fresh factors modestly improve pricing, but augmenting the stale model with the change in returns from updating stale portfolio assignments significantly improves pricing because the two components carry different pricing content. This reallocates abnormal returns, reverses the interpretation of thousands of event-study CARs, and reclassifies 14.7% of top-decile mutual funds. These findings reveal a fundamental structure in returns: a slow-moving component reflecting persistent fundamental risk and a fast-moving component capturing the arrival of information.

The Complexity Mirage

복잡한 예측 모델의 우위는 거래비용을 넣으면 사라진다

Complex return forecasters lose to simple ones once costs and longer windows enter.

Mesias Alfeus, Michael Jordan · Department of Statistics and Actuarial Science - Stellenbosch University and Stellenbosch University

  • KMZ(2024)의 '복잡할수록 좋다'를 남아공과 최근 미국에서 재검증
  • 랜덤 피처 릿지 머신과 단순 벤치마크 10개를 같은 조건으로 비교
  • 짧은 창에서는 복잡도가 이기지만 긴 창에 비용을 넣으면 진다
  • 신호는 진짜지만 상당 부분이 모멘텀 변수 하나에서 나온다
방법

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTKelly, Malamud and Zhou (2024, KMZ) show that highly complex prediction models can outperform simple ones when forecasting U.S. stock returns. We test this claim in two settings: the South African stock market, a smaller emerging market, and a shorter, more recent U.S. window (2017-2025) than KMZ's original sample, using the same random-feature ridge machine and ten simple benchmarks. Under KMZ's short-window design, accuracy in both countries rises with model complexity, as their theory predicts. Under a longer, more realistic window that includes trading costs and compares against the strongest simple alternative, however, the complex machine underperforms in both markets, losing to three simple models in South Africa and to the historical mean and a shrunk ridge regression in the United States. Placebo tests indicate the signal is genuine rather than spurious, but a large part of it traces to a single momentum variable, and accuracy deteriorates sharply once predictors are moderately noisy. A weaker version of the same pattern appears even in the developed market that motivated the original theory.

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTIn equity markets characterized by double-sided statutory transaction taxation-such as India's Securities Transaction Tax (STT), state stamp duties, and exchange levies-marginal rank turnover at portfolio inclusion boundaries imposes a persistent frictional drag on crosssectional factor strategies. In a conventional monthly momentum strategy selecting the top N = 30 equities, replacing rank N + 1 with rank N incurs two full execution fee legs (≈ 42.34 bps round-trip) to capture a momentum-score differential that is frequently negligible. We formalize and evaluate an asymmetric Hysteresis Rebalancing (Banded) framework on the Indian Nifty 500 universe using point-in-time constituent data from January 2018 through February 2026, with a primary out-of-sample evaluation period from January 2021 through December 2025 (T = 1, 260 contiguous out-of-sample trading days, evaluated over a 10-fold rolling-origin walk-forward protocol). Under this regime, new entrants must achieve a strict top N = 30 momentum rank, whereas incumbent holdings are retained as long as their score remains within an exploratory upper retention buffer (R t (i) ≤ B, for B ∈ {40, 45, 50, 60}). At B = 60, monthly position churn drops by 51.7% (from 9.57 to 4.62 stocks replaced per month), while net after-cost compound annual growth rate (CAGR) improves from 41.70% to 45.12% and the Sharpe ratio rises from 1.728 to 1.849, with maximum drawdown contracting from-26.44% to-25.41%. Although paired stationary bootstrap testing indicates that the after-cost Sharpe gain (∆Sharpe = +0.121, 95% CI [-0.048, +0.310], p = 0.167) is not statistically distinguishable from zero at conventional significance levels, the observed 51.7% reduction in position churn provides evidence that hysteresis banding can materially reduce execution burden in tax-intensive equity markets.

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTMany cross-sectional factors, such as industry-relative ratios, abnormal accruals, and the residual of a same-period regression, require the full cross-section of peer firms. Because firms file on staggered dates, a characteristic constructed shortly after a fiscal period closes is estimated from only those firms that have already reported. We term the resulting concern incomplete-cross-section leakage and assess whether it biases backtested performance. The conventional diagnostic, namely the disagreement between the early-filing signal and the complete-cross-section signal, does not identify the bias, because that disagreement combines three components: sampling variation from the smaller subsample, a difference in the covariate composition of the early filers, and any dependence of filing speed on the component of the signal under study. Only the third constitutes leakage. We isolate it by holding the covariate composition fixed, either through a matched control group or, equivalently, through the partial correlation between filing latency and the regression residual conditional on the regressors. This partial correlation is the selection-bias term of a Heckman model; because it is considerably less noisy than the disagreement statistic, we adopt it as the primary measure and provide it as an ex-ante screen, validated on a controlled experiment with a known planted bias. We apply the framework to two markets. For Taiwan, abnormal accruals and industry-adjusted inventory change exhibit no detectable leakage, and the associated long-short Sharpe ratio is bounded within 0.13. For the United States, where filing dates are observed directly through the SEC EDGAR system, profitability characteristics appear strongly distorted (filing latency correlates approximately-0.30 with industry-adjusted return on assets), yet the distortion is almost entirely attributable to firm size: larger firms file earlier and are more profitable, and conditioning on size reduces the partial correlation to approximately +0.09. The bias is therefore small in both markets, and the portion that remains operates through an observable characteristic that a size-aware release rule corrects. A companion paper develops that release rule; the present paper quantifies the magnitude of the bias it addresses.

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTMany financial signals are same-period cross-sectional estimates-industry-relative ratios, abnormal accruals, any characteristic defined as the residual of a peer-group regression. Because firms file on staggered dates, a signal computed shortly after a fiscal period closes is estimated on the early-filing subsample; when filing latency correlates with the regression disturbance, the estimate embeds forward-looking selection ("incomplete-cross-section leakage"), a channel that standard temporal train/test hygiene (purging, embargoing, as-of joins) does not address. Existing remedies are all-or-nothing: release at announcement (biased for susceptible signals) or withhold every signal until a statutory deadline (a blanket timeliness penalty). We present a release-control system that grades the required cross-sectional completeness per signal from a directly estimable susceptibility primitive-the partial correlation between filing latency and the complete-cross-section disturbance given the construction regressors. Benign signals release early; susceptible signals are withheld until the cross-section is complete enough to suppress selection bias, up to the deadline. On a known-truth simulation-with the susceptibility primitive fitted on prior completed periods and frozen before gating (no oracle)-the controller releases benign signals at 36-39% completeness (vs. a 35% floor) with no detectable systematic bias, and escalates strongly susceptible signals to the deadline endpoint, inheriting its zero bias (naive-release bias -0.39). The companion analysis (Wu and Wu, 2026b) shows on observed U.S. SEC filing timestamps that the primitive separates signals whose apparent distortion is benign observable composition from those with irreducible selection; here that separation drives the gate. The controller ships as a reference implementation and is designed to sit upstream of feature-store materialization.

The term is applied loosely to stocks, sectors, indices, even market conditions, which obscures the fact that published momentum definitions rest on beliefs, some incompatible, about how information reaches asset prices. Every variant outperformed the benchmark Nifty 500 TRI, seven by margins that survive cross-sectional overlap. But dispersion within the family is significant, both on return and downside behaviour. Second, an OLS combination of all five signals delivers essentially zero out-of-sample explanatory power, whereas a minimal composite of PPP, mean-reversion, and real-rate differentials generates a Sharpe ratio of +0.40 over 2005-2025 versus-0.24 for buy-and-hold USD. Third, a two-state Markov model identifies a persistent stress state occupying 27% of the sample in which USD/CHF depreciates at an annualized rate of-4.5%, and this state has been near-continuously active since 2022. The overall picture is consistent with the exchange-rate literature: theorymotivated single signals beat kitchen-sink combinations, and regime awareness is essential.

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTWe study whether nuclear and energy-adjacent equity options exhibit a harvestable variance risk premium. Using CRSP and OptionMetrics data for 2000-2024, we construct a systematic cash-secured short-put strategy on a curated universe of nuclear-related firms. The strategy compares at-the-money put implied volatility with GARCH-based realized volatility forecasts, then evaluates unconditional and IV/RV-filtered put-writing portfolios. The results show positive average option premia, high win rates, and substantially lower volatility than an equal-weight stock benchmark, though performance is measured before transaction costs and with a fixed universe.

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTMachine-learning volatility forecasts are usually judged by average out-of-sample accuracy, but their practical value depends on whether relative performance survives stress. This paper studies state-dependent forecast ranking rather than unconditional loss alone. Using the full 2,615-observation archived S&P 500 realized-volatility file preserved from the Oxford-Man Realized Library, I compare EWMA, HAR-RV, and XGBoost in a walk-forward design whose state thresholds use only information available through t-1. XGBoost outperforms HAR-RV in normal observations, but the ranking reverses under high volatility. The paired XGBoost-minus-HAR QLIKE differential is-0.0097 in normal states, +0.679 in Stress90, and +1.167 in Stress95; the Stress90-minus-Normal deterioration is +0.689. The pairwise reversal survives log-MSE and log-MAE, Holm adjustment, chronological subsamples, and a pre-specified top-5% one-day realizedvolatility-ratio state with 148 events. Moving-block bootstrap and leave-one-event-out diagnostics indicate that the jump-state result is not driven by any single observation, although the five largest events account for about 42% of the cumulative differential. By contrast, the primary Q50-to-Q90 transition definition identifies only eight events and remains descriptive under the pre-specified power gate. The evidence reveals a forecasting-risk paradox: a model can look competitive under unconditional average-error criteria while becoming materially worse when volatility is high or rising abruptly. The results motivate evaluating AI volatility forecasts by state-conditional ranking stability, not average accuracy alone.

Fama-French five-factormachine learningexcess return predictionmarket timingDJIAwalk-forward validation
ORIGINAL ABSTRACTThis study examines whether machine learning models can enhance the Fama-French five-factor asset pricing framework for predicting one-month-ahead excess returns of the thirty constituent stocks of the Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJIA). Two complementary modeling tracks are developed. The first frames the task as a regression problem, predicting the numerical value of next-month excess return using Linear Regression, a Multilayer Perceptron (MLP), a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN, implemented with Gated Recurrent Units), and a Transformer built from stacked multi-head self-attention layers. The second frames the task as a binary classification problem, predicting the direction (up or down) of next-month excess return using Logistic Regression, Random Forest, MLP, RNN, and Transformer architectures adapted for classification. All models are trained and evaluated using a walk-forward protocol on data spanning December 1989 through June 2026, combining Fama-French factors with macroeconomic indicators from the Federal Reserve Economic Data (FRED) database. Model outputs are converted into long/cash market-timing signals and evaluated using the Sharpe ratio of an equal-weighted 30-stock portfolio over five trailing horizons (1, 3, 5, 10, and 20 years), benchmarked against (i) a passive buy-and-hold portfolio of the same 30 stocks, and (ii) the actual DJIA index.

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTWe show that the optimal dynamic portfolio policy under conditional mean-variance preferences is w * t ∝ µt/σ 2 t , not the pure inverse-volatility rule wt ∝ 1/σ 2 t popularized by Moreira and Muir (2017). Constructing the general policy directly, using a 12-month trailing conditional-mean estimator, we find it earns a higher alpha than the pure rule (7.94% versus 5.65% annualized), but a lower Sharpe ratio and higher turnover.

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTI study returns to leveraged single stock ETFs (LSS-ETFs), decomposing the return shortfall relative to a simple benchmark into a component attributable to daily rebalancing trades and one attributable to frictions such as fees, trading costs, and excess loan margins. For my main sample comprised of thirty-five ETFs introduced since June 2022, LSS-ETFs underperform by an average of 0.75% per month, with 0.20% attributable to daily rebalancing and 0.55% to frictions. For a supplemental sample of 235 ETFs listed since April 2024 long levered single stock ETFs underperform by an average of 1.47% per month, with 0.42% attributable to daily rebalancing and 1.04% to frictions. Consistent with theory, rebalancing costs are negatively related to return serial correlation as captured by return variance ratios and positively related to daily volatility. Analysis of a broader sample of hypothetical single-stock ETF returns over the past fifty years reveals that LSS-ETFs underperform on average when return volatility is high, not due to volatility per se, but because high volatility periods are characterized by return reversals. Some results reported here are extracted from a prior working paper titled "Returns to Constant Leverage Strategies: General Principles and Application to Levered Single-Stock ETFs."

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTA growing literature reports that machine-learning (ML) models deliver large cross-sectional stock-selection gains, yet whether those gains are implementable rather than merely statistical remains contested. We revisit tree-ensemble stock selection in Taiwan, an Asia-Pacific market sharply segmented between liquid Taiwan Stock Exchange (TWSE) large-caps and thinly traded Taipei Exchange (TPEx/OTC) small-caps. To limit survivorship bias, we reconstruct the investable universe at each annual May formation from official exchange files, retaining firms that later delist. Over 2011–2024, tree ensembles predict top-quintile next-year returns, and we form equal- and value-weighted top-ten portfolios. Unconstrained, the random forest earns 44.6% per year against 7.9% for the Yuanta Taiwan Top-50 ETF (0050) and 6.4% for the index (TAIEX). This advantage is confined to the hard-to-trade segment. A modest NT$100 million liquidity floor turns the random-forest return negative (−1.3%); value-weighting lowers but does not remove it, so the binding constraint is the selectable universe, not the weighting scheme. Within the tradable universe the ranking skill (AUC) falls to about 0.50 and the monthly-based annualized Sharpe ratio is 0.02 against 1.29 unconstrained. Restricting selection to the main board roughly halves the return (44.6% to 23.5%), and economic capacity is only about NT$0.2–0.4 million. The collapse survives higher-capacity gradient boosting, a wide neural network, and an enriched feature set, so it reflects the investable opportunity set rather than an underpowered model: we read the evidence as liquidity-confined predictive structure rather than investable alpha.

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTClassical option-hedging methods like Black-Scholes delta assume constant, free rebalancing, which real markets don't allow. Deep hedging trains a neural network to handle these frictions directly, and prior work reports strong results. But those comparisons usually pit deep hedging against a frictionless classical baseline on simulated price data. That's not a fair fight, and it leaves open whether the advantage is real. We test this using five years of actual BTC options data from Deribit (2020-2024), comparing Black-Scholes delta, Leland's cost-adjusted hedge, and the Whalley-Wilmott no-trade band against three deep hedging setups: an LSTM and a feedforward network, each trained with a CVaR loss and, in some runs, a penalty for trading too often. All six strategies face the same 5 basis point transaction cost. On 11,546 test episodes from September 2023 to December 2024, Whalley-Wilmott cuts transaction costs significantly versus hourly rebalancing, saving $1.79 per episode against plain BS delta (95% CI [-2.21, -1.39], p < 0.0001) by trading about eight times less often. Its P&L and tail-risk numbers are better too, though not quite significant at this sample size. None of the three deep hedging models beat any classical benchmark on any metric, and all kept trading almost every hour regardless of penalty weight, a twenty-fold range barely moved the needle. A calmer validation period shows Whalley-Wilmott's P&L edge shrinks or disappears there while its cost edge holds, so the result depends on market regime. We think the likely causes are a small training set and the lack of any built-in mechanism for sitting still in the architectures tested. Not a flashy result, but an honest one: a real-data check on a claim mostly supported by simulations so far.

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTU.S. equity returns are known to be higher overnight, on Fridays, in January, around the turn of the month, and during macroeconomic announcement windows. We replicate 153 long-short factors and document the mirror image of these patterns: factor premia are systematically lower in exactly the same periods. On average, a factor loses 2.01 bps overnight but earns 5.45 bps intraday; it earns 5.77 bps on Mondays versus 1.24 bps on Fridays; and its returns are significantly lower in January, at the turn of the month, and around macroeconomic announcements. The reversed calendar effects persist out of sample and strengthen when news sentiment is elevated, consistent with sentiment-driven mispricing.

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTInstitutional quantitative equity frameworks routinely mandate sector concentration limits or industry neutrality to eliminate uncompensated macroeconomic sector bets. While developedmarket long-short literature often supports neutralization, recent asset pricing theory [e.g., 6] demonstrates that long-only factor portfolios are systematically impaired by sector constraints because shorting decaying industries is disallowed. We provide an out-of-sample empirical investigation of this hypothesis in the Indian equity market using point-in-time National Stock Exchange (NSE) Nifty 500 constituent data across an 8-year historical sample (January 1, 2018 to February 26, 2026). Evaluating four parametric sector-cap regimes (C ∈ {2, 3, 4, 5}) and one sector-balanced selection regime against an unconstrained benchmark across 10 contiguous out-of-sample evaluation folds (1260 trading days / 5.0 trading years) under realistic transaction costs (42.34 bps round-trip friction including Securities Transaction Tax, stamp duty, exchange levies, and assumed 10 bps execution slippage), we document that all evaluated constrained configurations produce lower realized compound returns and Sharpe ratios than the unconstrained benchmark. An unconstrained 30-stock volatility-adjusted momentum strategy delivers an out-of-sample CAGR of 42.56% and a Sharpe ratio of 1.728. Capping sector allocations to 3 stocks compresses the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI) from 0.169 to 0.084, but reduces CAGR to 33.97% (a-8.59pp annual drag) and Sharpe to 1.497 (unadjusted bootstrap p = 0.0204; Holm-adjusted bootstrap p = 0.1020; JKM p = 0.0281), with no improvement in maximum drawdown (-26.79% vs.-26.44%). We find evidence consistent with a factor dilution mechanism: sector caps exclude high-conviction momentum leaders in trending macro sectors, replacing them with lower-ranked securities from lagging industries (average selected momentum rank deteriorates from 15.5 to 48.2), which is positively associated with subsequent relative performance drag in Newey-West HAC predictive regressions (t = 2.41, p = 0.018).

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTWe report a structured negative result together with the narrow positive result that survives beside it. A fivefactor composite equity screen over the Nasdaq-100, whose weights were set heuristically, is decomposed into two disjoint parameter groups: composite weights, three of whose five factors derive from an undated fundamentals snapshot, and price-derived selection gates, which are point-in-time clean. We prove that the first group is not identified in our data: a factor constant in time contributes a time-invariant column to the design matrix and cannot be separated from the intercept by any pooled estimator. Non-negative least squares on these data place 92% of fitted weight on the volatility term and return unstable zero sets that do not coincide with the contaminated factors; we report these fits as uninformative rather than as confirmation, and out-of-sample R 2 reaches-0.314. We therefore decline to tune the weights, and confirm by direct search that no re-weighting is supportable: across 69 overlapping score dates (2020-08 to 2026-05, ≈ 23 effective independent windows), with Newey-West and Hansen-Hodrick standard errors and a Romano-Wolf stepdown correction replacing the naive paired t, no perturbation to any weight attains significance; the largest effect (removing the earnings-revision factor, t NW =-2.37) has a stepdown-adjusted p = 0.156. The second group is identifiable, and a walk-forward grid search over it produced the one defensible parameter change in this study, tightening the momentum gate from +25% to +15% and raising the full-sample longshort spread from +2.67% (t = 3.20) to +4.73% (t = 4.13), with the gate value selected in 100% of walkforward folds. A second optimization pass against the updated baseline yields no further uplift (-0.09%, t =-0.15), which we interpret as convergence rather than failure. We argue the separability diagnosis-asking which parameters the data can speak to before asking what their values should be-is the transferable contribution.

market regime detectionK-Means clusteringPCAregime forecastingpersistence benchmarktactical asset allocation
ORIGINAL ABSTRACTThis paper investigates whether unsupervised machine learning can identify economically meaningful regimes in the US equity market and whether such regimes provide genuine forecasting or investment value. Using a daily dataset of 3,823 observations spanning 18 October 2010 to 31 December 2025, sixteen standardized market, volatility, and macro-financial features are reduced via Principal Component Analysis (eight components explaining 92.1% of variance) and partitioned using K-Means clustering, validated against a Gaussian Mixture Model. The optimal solution, selected by silhouette score, identifies two statistically and economically distinct regimes, subsequently labelled Bull / Low-Risk (n = 3,201; 83.7% of observations) and Bear / High-Risk (n = 622; 16.3%). The regimes differ significantly across mean return, volatility, VIX level, momentum, and drawdown (Welch t-tests, all p < .001; Cohen's d up to 2.94), and exhibit strong persistence, with Bull-to-Bull and Bear-to-Bear transition probabilities of 96.5% and 81.8% respectively. A chronological, one-step-ahead out-of-sample forecasting exercise compares Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and Gradient Boosting classifiers against a naive persistence benchmark ("tomorrow's regime equals today's regime"). The persistence benchmark achieved the highest out-of-sample accuracy (93.55%), exceeding Random Forest (91.89%), Logistic Regression (89.80%), and Gradient Boosting (89.01%). This finding does not support the hypothesis that supervised machine learning provides superior next-day regime forecasting relative to a simple persistence rule. A regime-conditioned tactical investment strategy (fully invested in Bull, fully divested in Bear, signal lagged by one day, 10 basis point transaction costs) reduced maximum drawdown relative to buy-and-hold (-28.20% versus-33.92%) but underperformed on both compound annual growth rate (5.80% versus 12.68%) and Sharpe ratio (0.546 versus 0.780). Forward-return analysis indicates that returns following Bear/High-Risk observations were, on average, higher than returns following Bull/Low-Risk observations at 1-, 5-, and 20-day horizons, offering a plausible explanation for the strategy's return shortfall despite its lower drawdown. The study concludes that regime identification is statistically robust and economically interpretable, but that regime identification is not equivalent to reliable regime forecasting or to superior risk-adjusted investment performance. The paper's contribution lies in this explicit separation of unsupervised classification, supervised forecasting, and economic usefulness-three distinct questions that are frequently conflated in applied machine learning finance research. A supplementary robustness check (Section XI.J), which widens the feature set to twenty-nine variables by restoring the raw price, volume, and moving-average series the main specification deliberately excludes, produces a weaker four-regime solution and a severe train/test distribution shift that collapses out-of-sample forecasting performance-a negative result that, if anything, reinforces the original feature-exclusion rationale in Section IV.

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTBoth practitioner commentary and the academic literature emphasize a negative relation between the volatility of returns and outcomes to constant leverage investment strategies such as leveraged ETFs (LETFs). I demonstrate that there is no hardwired negative relation in expectation. Rather, return serial covariances as captured by the return “Variance Ratio” are crucial; volatility increases average LETF returns in the presence of positive serial correlation and vice versa, and has no effect if returns are serially uncorrelated. In the presence of serial dependence, there are asymmetries in expected rebalancing costs across leveraged long vs. inverse strategies. However, return volatility widens the gap between expected and median compound LETF returns, because of increased skewness. The equations contained herein are extracted from a prior working paper titled "Returns to Constant Leverage Strategies: General Principles and Application to Leveraged Single-Stock ETFs."

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTWe re-estimate canonical option-implied predictability evidence using a unified 2015--2026 panel of 12.36 million U.S. equity firm-day observations across 10,026 underlyings. We split the sample into three regimes: late-post-crisis low volatility (2015--2019), high-volatility transition (2020--2022), and AI/mega-cap concentration (2023--2026). The Xing et al. (2010) smirk--return relationship weakens steadily: the next-month univariate smirk coefficient falls from $-0.023$ $(t=-5.5)$ in 2015--2019 to an insignificant $-0.006$ $(t=-1.5)$ in 2023--2026, and turns positive at the three-month horizon $(+0.016,\ t=+2.1)$. In joint specifications with all six canonical signals, the smirk is insignificant throughout and again changes sign in the latest regime. By contrast, the Cremers--Weinbaum IV spread and a Bakshi et al. (2003)-style risk-neutral skewness measure remain significant across regimes and specifications. A boosted-tree benchmark using IV-surface, trading-activity, Greeks, and liquidity features outperforms linear models for next-month return prediction only in the AI/mega-cap regime, with $R^2_{\mathrm{OOS}}=+1.29%$ versus $+0.07%$. Permutation importance identifies different leading predictors by regime, and no canonical hand-engineered signal enters the top five. For firm-level five-day crash classification, AUC is highest in calm markets $(0.706,\ \text{XGBoost})$ and lowest during the high-volatility transition $(0.561)$. Overall, option-implied predictability is real but regime-dependent, and the post-2023 AI/mega-cap period differs sharply from the pre-COVID setting in which the canonical results were established.

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTThis article examines various methods of constructingmultidimensional probabilistic forecasts of electricity prices. Building on the Multiple Split (MS) method, it incorporates forecast averaging across estimation windows of different lengths and compares its performance with that of other, well-established methods. The research demonstrates that the ensemble representation of the price distribution is particularly useful in battery energy storage system (BESS) management. It enables the direct construction of probabilistic forecasts of daily profits. These forecasts can be used to determine optimal charging and discharging hours, as well as to support risk management decisions. The methods are evaluated using data from the German and Spanish day-ahead electricity markets from 2021-2024. The results indicate that theMS method with averaging (MS-ave) generally outperforms the other considered approaches in terms of Prediction Interval Coverage Probability (PICP), the Continuous Ranked Probability Score (CRPS) and the Energy Score (ES). Moreover, it is superior in supporting BESS trading strategies, particularly in case of non-zero operational costs.

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTAlgorithmic trading now represents a market exceeding $20 billion, where even marginal gains in signal robustness can translate into economically significant returns. Existing evaluations of equity prediction models do not explicitly target regime robustness during hyperparameter selection. Five model classes are trained on daily observations from approximately 300 large-cap US equities over eleven years, with Bayesian optimisation configured to target trading performance across three statistically different market regimes. Regime-robust hyperparameter selection is associated with out-of-sample generalisation, as signal precision remains above the random baseline across all four quarters of the test period, and portfolio performance slowly degrades under simulated input noise before collapsing beyond a defined threshold. No individual tabular deep learning architecture outperforms gradient-boosted trees, but combining XGBoost and TabNet using rank aggregation produces a Hybrid ensemble with an annualised return of 51.26%, a Sharpe ratio of 2.44, and a statistically significant CAPM alpha of 0.423 (p = 0.011). A near-zero beta indicates this outperformance is driven by stock selection, not market exposure. Alternative data plays a secondary role once technical and fundamental features are accounted for, as well as contributing more strongly on the short side than the long, and varies by model class. An interactive application makes these results explorable in real time, with live data integration the remaining step toward practical deployment.

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTTime-series momentum stands as one of the most reliable and heavily backtested anomalies in quantitative finance, serving as a foundational alpha source for modern managed futures and trend-following strategies. However, a recent academic paper by Matti Suominen and Erik Hjalmarsson, titled "Boundaries of Time Series Momentum," uncovers a structural vulnerability that every practitioner must account for. The authors demonstrate that while equity market trends persist reliably during normal business cycles, they systematically break down and aggressively reverse when market valuations reach historical extremes. This phenomenon establishes clear macro "boundaries" where chasing the trend shifts from a highly profitable strategy to a severe drawdown risk.

trade durationsACD modelscore-drivenheapinghigh-frequency FXgeneralized gamma
ORIGINAL ABSTRACTTrade durations in high-frequency foreign exchange data exhibit increased occurrence near integer values. To address this empirical phenomenon, we propose the granularity-adjusted autoregressive conditional duration (GA-ACD) model. It is based on a novel two-component mixture distribution consisting of a standard generalized gamma component for regular durations and a second component that locally redistributes probability mass around integer values to capture heaping. Conditional dynamics are modeled within a score-driven framework, allowing the scale parameter to vary over time in response to past durations, and enabling maximum likelihood estimation of all model parameters. A simulation study shows that ignoring heaping leads to biased parameter estimates and distorted inference regarding both the distribution and the dynamics of durations. An empirical analysis demonstrates that integer-duration clustering is pervasive across major currency pairs and that the GA-ACD model outperforms the standard generalized gamma ACD model.

short-sale constraintssecurities lendingretail investorsprice discoveryanomaliesdifference-in-differences
ORIGINAL ABSTRACTThis paper studies whether fintech innovation can relax short-sale constraints and improve price discovery. I examine Robinhood's May 2022 stock lending program, which mobilized dispersed retail shareholdings into the securities-lending market. Using a difference-indifferences design, I find evidence that the program relaxes short-sale constraints for stocks heavily owned by retail investors. Short interest rises by 0.43 percentage points among stocks more exposed to the program. Further evidence suggests that Robinhood helps bring retail-held shares into the lending market, increasing lendable supply outside the traditional institutional lending pool. I also find suggestive evidence of improved price discovery: anomaly-related pricing errors decline more among stocks exposed to the program, with larger declines on the short than on the long side for several anomalies. Overall, the evidence suggests that fintech innovation can relax limits to arbitrage and improve price discovery by making dispersed shareholdings easier to intermediate into the securities-lending market.

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTInstitutional investors commonly separate strategic asset allocation (SAA) from tactical asset allocation (TAA). This governance structure is practical, but repeated one-period tactical optimization can be dynamically suboptimal when positions persist, signals evolve, and changing exposure is costly. We develop a discrete-time benchmark-relative model with an evolving strategic reference, tactical return predictors, quadratic trading costs, and a discounted recursive entropic criterion for continuation-value uncertainty. The optimal policy trades partially toward a forward-looking dynamic aim portfolio. In a scalar benchmark, we derive an exact persistence threshold separating attenuation from amplification of current tactical signals relative to one-period TAA. In a transitory-predictor setting, greater uncertainty about future predictor realizations reduces the signal-driven aim but increases the adjustment rate toward it, lowering the net current signal response. We also characterize trading-cost effects, obtaining general multivariate value and action-penalty orderings and sharper directional policy results in scalar or aligned settings. We distinguish one-step action loss from the full recursive loss generated by repeatedly following a suboptimal policy, derive exact fixed-policy and policy-loss identities, and use them to choose the best rule within a restricted, governance-compatible two-step SAA-TAA family. Numerical illustrations show that value-based calibration can materially improve a simple institutional rule even when coefficient proximity to the dynamic optimum is a poor guide to economic performance.

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTFinancial direction prediction is difficult because return distributions are non-stationary, crossasset relationships drift across regimes, and modern classifiers can be substantially overconfident. This paper documents HPT-DTE, a hybrid architecture that combines a time-domain neural sequence encoder, an FFT-based frequency-domain branch, decision-tree regime conditioning, a logistic meta-learner, and held-out isotonic calibration. For an asset, a 20-day window of twelve backward-looking technical and macroeconomic features is transformed into two representations. Time tokens receive a learnable phase-shift tensor, while real and imaginary FFT coefficients provide a harmonic representation. Multi-head cross-attention uses the time branch as query and the frequency branch as key/value; a learned sigmoid gate controls the harmonic residual. A shallow regime tree supplies a one-hot leaf condition, and an equity tree contributes an independent probability to a regularized meta-learner. The calibrated probability is converted into a selective decision with an abstention band. The reported experiment trains on nine equities during 2017-2023 and evaluates without fine-tuning on four unseen equities, three cryptocurrencies, and GLD during 2024-2026. The selective accuracy is 60.0% on TSLA and 51.4-53.6% on the three cryptocurrencies, with 22-46 predictions among 80 evaluation opportunities per asset. We provide mathematical descriptions, proofs of the calibration and selectivity properties, implementationgrounded interpretation, and a candid audit of limitations, including the distinction between trade-conditioned accuracy and unconditional forecasting accuracy.

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTMarket risk premium forecasts are traditionally evaluated through point forecasts of expected returns, implicitly treating the conditional expectation as a sufficient representation of future uncertainty. This paper examines whether evaluating predictive distributions alongside point forecasts provides additional information for portfolio allocation and risk management. Predictive distributions are generated using a simulation-based geometric Brownian motion framework and evaluated using both statistical and economic criteria. Consistent with the return predictability literature, the conditional expectation exhibits limited forecasting power. The predictive distributions, however, are reasonably well calibrated and satisfy several standard density forecast evaluation criteria. Portfolio analyses indicate that while expectation-based strategies generate the highest terminal wealth and strongest conventional risk-adjusted performance, distribution-based strategies substantially reduce volatility, drawdowns, and tail-risk exposure. The results suggest that forecasting models should be evaluated not only by the accuracy of their point forecasts, but also by how effectively they characterize the uncertainty surrounding future outcomes.

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTWe examine whether a pooled model or a segmented model more accurately forecasts next-month corporate-bond liquidity. Using TRACE transactions from 2004 to 2024, we construct a Panel Tree that retains splits when segmented forecasts reduce validation MAE. Segmentation raises linear-model out-of-sample R^2 from 1-3% to about 24%, narrowing the gap with pooled nonlinear models, and lowers nonlinear-model MAE. ORIGINAL ABSTRACTA common heuristic among index-options traders holds that sudden shifts in open interest (OI) around a price level serve as an early warning of an impending breakout. This paper tests that heuristic against a full year of NIFTY 50 index options data using a fully specified, auditable pipeline: a dynamic, threshold-based swing detector identifies intraday Break-of-Structure and Change-of-Character events at two reversal thresholds. We test three nested hypotheses. H1 (association): the PE-minus-CE open-interest differential around a break is strongly associated with break direction, a result that survives Bonferroni correction across a large battery of tests and is robust to the choice of strike band and OI-measurement window. A placebo/negative-control test addresses a specific concern with H1: that OI might simply track any sufficiently large price move, with confirmed-break status adding nothing on its own. Against magnitude-matched non-break moments, confirmed-break status is associated with a further, incremental OI reaction beyond move size alone, an effect concentrated in smaller moves and narrowing, but not disappearing, as move size grows. H2 (event-time lead-lag pattern, not a causal test): the association builds steadily in the minutes before confirmation and continues strengthening for a few minutes after, then partially declines and plateaus, the signature of a reactive rather than anticipatory relationship. H3 (tradable edge): a real-time predictive signal, conditioned to remove the confound of an already-underway price move, showed an apparently genuine in-sample edge, significant at the conventional level though materially weaker once trades are aggregated to account for within-day dependence. Every parameter of this signal was then locked and applied, without refitting, to a genuinely held-out Jan–Apr 2026 sample. The signal did not hold up out-of-sample, a pattern that is robust across five alternative definitions of the “quiet” conditioning subset used to isolate the signal from the price move it is trying to anticipate. We also went back to two specific null tests written earlier in this project, originally run on an Oct 2025–Apr 2026 dataset, and reran them against our Jan–Jul 2025 data, which those scripts had never touched. On the whole, we find no robust evidence that intraday OI repositioning provides advance predictive information about structural price breaks in this setting. The evidence instead supports interpreting OI repositioning as a state variable of an ongoing price-discovery process, informative about what is happening rather than what will happen next, and not as a forecasting signal.

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTPortfolio constraints are known to act as implicit shrinkage on an estimated covariance matrix. We show that the same constraints also compress the differences across the portfolios implied by competing covariance models, so that weight restrictions operate as a form of shrinkage across models rather than within a single estimate. As a consequence, once constraints are in place, the equally weighted 1/M combination of covariance forecasts performs on par with the best individual model, and it does so without requiring the practitioner to identify the best model in advance. We formalize this mechanism analytically by showing that the variance cost of the 1/M rule relative to the oracle-optimal combination vanishes as the cross-sectional dimension grows. Monte Carlo simulations and an empirical application to equity data with up to 1,000 stocks support these predictions. Our findings suggest that, for managers operating under the constraints they typically face, such as no-short-sales or concentration constraints, the cost of forgoing covariance model selection is small.

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTFunding rates on perpetual futures are directional transfers, yet empirical work often enters them as absolute values. That convention can hide an economically relevant asymmetry. This paper returns to the frozen Binance BTCUSDT and ETHUSDT tape from 2020-2026 and separates lagged positive funding from the magnitude of negative funding, while leaving the increment-variance and pre-averaged apparent-H estimators unchanged. In the signed-basis specification, a one-standard-deviation increase in positive funding is associated with coefficients of-0.0058 and-0.0052 for Bitcoin and-0.0042 and-0.0041 for Ether; each remains significant after Holm adjustment. The corresponding negative-side 90% confidence intervals fall within approximately ±0.0013. Two one-sided tests also establish equivalence to zero at the disclosed, sensitivity-tested ±0.0015 benchmark. The asymmetry persists in raw units, under equal state weighting and conditional-state estimation, across alternative HAC bandwidths, and in a 499-replication 28-day moving-block bootstrap. Signed basis controls do not absorb it, and the 2020-2022 and 2023-2026 estimates show no formal break. By contrast, signed funding-by-settlement interactions and signed block-extreme coefficients fail to survive familywise-error correction. The evidence places the positive-funding result inside the increment-variance measurement family: it is a persistent observation-state association, rather than evidence about latent spot regularity, long-side inventory, causal leverage, transition information, or a trading rule.

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTWe propose a new methodology to estimate the equity term structure. Instead of using realized returns of dividend assets, we generalize the implied cost of capital approach and imply the term structure of ex-ante expected returns from the cross-section of observed stock prices and projected firm-level cash flows. Using US data for 1980-2024, we find an unconditionally upward sloping term structure of risk premia with rich cross-sectional patterns in the size, value and credit risk dimensions. Strikingly, value firms and speculative-grade firms have flat or even downward-sloping term structures. We also detect that the term structure flattens out in recessions.

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTRecent advances in LLM agents enable a new paradigm for asset pricing, which we call Agentic Empirical Asset Pricing (AEAP): systems that autonomously conduct the scientific discovery process itself. We define AEAP and identify its core building blocks. Existing evaluation practices backtest only the outputs (factors or trades), not the autonomous discovery system that produced them. We focus on factor discovery, contributing a reference architecture, a rigorous evaluation standard for discovered factors, and a method for out-of-sample backtesting the discovery system. As a concrete instance of that architecture, we evaluate SEADS against five re-implemented baselines on two US equity panels using this standard: no single metric ranks the systems consistently, motivating evaluation on multiple axes at once. A separate rolling re-execution then asks the complementary question of whether the discovery process itself, not one static output, is reliable. We also report negative findings and limitations that surface further evaluation pitfalls for future AEAP systems.

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTAverage strategy performance is one of the most common shortcuts in portfolio research. It gives the researcher a clean benchmark, a single reference line, and a simple way to compare one strategy against a broader group of similar strategies. In many cases, this is useful. But it can also be misleading. The problem is that an average hides dispersion. Two peer groups can have the same average return, but the internal structure of those groups can be completely different. In one year, nearly all strategies may behave similarly and cluster around the median. In another year, the same average may hide a wide spread between winners and losers. For portfolio construction, this distinction matters. This case study shows how Quantpedia API can be used to go beyond the average peer group return and measure yearly performance dispersion across a group of trend-following strategies. The goal is not only to ask how the average strategy performed, but also how different the individual strategies were from each other.

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTDigital attention is widely used as an input in financial models, but different data sources may lead to different conclusions. We test whether financial findings remain stable when the attention proxy is replaced while the sample, timing, outcomes, estimator, and inferential framework are held constant. Using Google Trends, Wikipedia pageviews, GDELT news intensity, and consensus measures for 57 US firms from 2016 to 2025, we examine trading volume, forward volatility, contemporaneous and forward returns, attention around earnings announcements, and out-of-sample forecasting. Volume and earnings-event conclusions remain stable across sources. Forward-volatility effects are consistently positive but differ in inferential strength, whereas return effects are small, sign-unstable, and provide no out-of-sample forecasting gains. These results show that strong empirical relationships are robust to reasonable measurement choices, while weaker findings are more source-dependent. We therefore treat data-source selection as a component of model uncertainty and propose controlled proxy substitution as a diagnostic for inferential fragility in intelligent financial systems.

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTDecentralized physical infrastructure networks (DePINs) are increasingly presented as investable exposure to the computing, connectivity, and energy infrastructure underpinning articial intelligence. We examine whether this narrative is reected in market prices or whether DePIN tokens behave primarily as crypto-risk assets. Using 1,065 common trading days from May 2022 to August 2026, we analyze functionally selected DePIN tokens alongside semiconductors, utilities, uranium, natural gas, Bitcoin, and Ether. The empirical design combines dynamic connectedness with xed-dimension factor ltering to distinguish infrastructure-related transmission from common crypto-market exposure, followed by out-of-sample portfolio tests of its economic relevance. Bitcoin and Ether dominate shock transmission. Filtering common crypto exposure reduces connectedness among the thematic assets from 36.3% to 20.0%, while broader market controls lower it to 17.8%, leaving only a modest residual DePIN-infrastructure channel. This linkage is strongly state dependent, increasing approximately vefold in both market tails relative to the median, and 90.95% of its absolute magnitude is concentrated within one to ve trading days. A stricter compute-only specication restricted to Render Network (RENDER) and Akash Network (AKT) produces the same economic classication. Moreover, adding DePIN tokens to physical-infrastructure portfolios generates no robust out-of-sample improvement in risk-adjusted performance. The results show that protocol function does not automatically translate into nancial exposure to the underlying infrastructure: the studied DePIN tokens behave predominantly as cryptorisk assets with a modest, state-dependent, and transient infrastructure component.

Method

GARCH-MIDASDCC-MIDASsector correlationminimum spanning treeinflation regimesEuropean equities
ORIGINAL ABSTRACTInflation is a major source of macro-financial uncertainty, with potentially heterogeneous implications for sectoral equity risk and co-movement. We examine whether inflation is associated with low-frequency volatility in European equity sectors and document how estimated long-run dependence and network topology vary across changing inflation conditions over 2000–2025. Using indices for Energy, Financials, Industrials, Consumer Discretionary, and Consumer Staples, we estimate sector-specific GJR-GARCH-MIDAS models in which inflation enters the low-frequency variance component. We use the resulting standardized residuals to estimate long-run correlations through a DCC-MIDAS model. We then derive an Average Correlation Index (ACI) from the estimated correlations and construct minimum spanning trees (MSTs) from the corresponding correlation-based distances. Inflation is positively associated with low-frequency volatility in the Energy, Financials, Industrials, and Consumer Discretionary sectors, but the association is not statistically significant in the Consumer Staples sector. The estimated long-run correlations are highly persistent, reflecting an extended history of realized dependence. We map the ACI and MSTs onto inflationary and disinflationary episodes identified ex post. The ACI varies across changing inflation conditions but does not exhibit a monotonic relationship with inflation. Network topology adds information beyond average correlation, with Industrials central in most episodes, cyclical sectors forming a tighter core during the 2021–2023 energy-shock episode, and the network becoming more chain-like during the 2024–2025 disinflation period. These findings show that similar levels of average correlation can mask materially different configurations of persistent sectoral dependence, with implications for diversification, risk budgeting, stress testing, and the monitoring of shock-transmission channels.

FOMCprediction marketsCME FedWatchimplied probabilitiesmarket microstructuremonetary policy expectations
ORIGINAL ABSTRACTAs forecasts of 18 FOMC decisions, the CME FedWatch tool and a prediction market that prices each decision outcome directly are statistically inseparable, yet the two name a different most likely decision in 2.08 percent of minutes, in episodes of up to 64 hours. The difference lies in what each can express. FedWatch carries exactly one number per meeting, the expected policy change; every published probability follows mechanically from it, and its step size is fixed by the futures contract and the FOMC calendar before any trading occurs. A single price step can shift the published probability by up to 4.4 percentage points. The prediction market prices the outcomes themselves, every minute, around the clock. The disagreements are real. The two markets price different means, and the tool's arithmetic creates almost none of the disagreements. We publish the market series, the code that rebuilds the standard tool, and every disagreement with its timestamp.

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTFor twenty years the argument over whether portfolio optimization beats equal weighting has gone unresolved. We show that both sides are right on their own data. What divides them is the menu of assets on offer. On the menu a real equity investor can reach, twenty-eight long-only regional factor indices, no optimization rule beats equal weighting by a margin this much data can settle. We race seventeen rules over 210 months out of sample, testing every comparison for significance. The optimizers are not at fault: these indices are close to being the same bet. Long-only factor tilts within a region move almost in lockstep, so the whole menu carries barely more independent risk than one index, and no weighting scheme can manufacture diversification the menu does not contain. Three asset classes, Treasuries, gold and cash, add more of it than all twenty-eight equity indices combined. For a retail investor, widening the menu is the only move with measurable evidence.

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTWe estimate a two-state Gaussian-mixture hidden Markov model for daily Brent crude, gold, silver, and natural gas futures in which transition probabilities depend on lagged geopolitical risk (GPR). Using the threat and act components of the daily GPR index, we find that realised geopolitical acts are associated with greater stress-regime persistence: a one-standard-deviation increase in act elevation is associated with roughly 45 to 51 percent higher odds of remaining stressed. Threat effects are concentrated on entry from calm but are weaker and not robust to the full control set. Nested likelihoodratio tests reject dropping the geopolitical block from the transition kernel. The results indicate that the geopolitical association is strongest through regime duration rather than through a simple level effect on volatility.

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTMarket commentary often compresses a rise in Japanese government bond yields into a single causal chain: yen funding becomes more expensive, carry trades unwind, and global risk assets reprice. This paper tests the empirical content of that label. Using daily Japanese yield-curve innovations, a 12-currency exposure panel, and a separately constructed non-yen high-minus-low carry factor from 2013 through July 2026, the design separates short-end from long-duration shocks, positive from negative repricing, and high-from normal-volatility states. The carry-unwind signature is sharply conditional. In the currency panel, positive short-end shocks produce a stronger five-day loss gradient among economies with larger predetermined yen-credit exposure only in high-volatility states; the interaction survives Holm correction (p = 0.018), and the positive-minus-negative high-volatility contrast also survives (p = 0.010). In the separately constructed carry factor, the total slope on positive short-end repricing is negative at one and five days in high-volatility states, with Holm-adjusted p-values of 0.016 and 0.018. Negative short-end and long-duration shocks are close to zero. Event paths are directionally consistent but weaker: funding-type shocks are followed by a 1.51% twenty-day carry loss versus 0.31% after duration-type shocks, with a suggestive difference (p = 0.064). A 90th-percentile volatility threshold and release-lag checks preserve the main ordering. The evidence supports a state-contingent classification, not a generic causal claim: carry unwind is not a synonym for rising JGB yields.

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTWe study the quadratic tracking problem of a general stochastic target process with absolutely continuous controls, with and without terminal constraint. We derive explicit, non-asymptotic upper bounds in terms of a Besov-type modulus of the target. These bounds yield sharp explicit rates that specialize to the square-root order for semimartingale targets. We then apply these results to a generalized Obizhaeva--Wang execution model with random terminal inventory. We first develop a Hilbert-space approach to characterize its optimal strategy, which includes jumps. To avoid such trading spikes, one regularizes the problem by a quadratic trading-rate penalty with coefficient $\varepsilon$. We then show that the regularized optimal execution cost---and therefore the excess price impact cost of the regularized optimal strategy---converges at the sharp rate $O(\sqrt{\varepsilon})$. Since the regularized optimal strategy is not available in closed form, we further construct a nearly optimal strategy which is readily implementable and shares the same approximation rate.

With zero firm-specific slack, the common-map scale changes the certified variance reduction but not the normalized allocation, which depends only on observed information geometry. The lower in-sample variance ranking relative to equal risk also appears across the reported frozen language-model representations. The framework therefore distribution-valued firm information into a coherent risk bound and an implementable allocation rule constructed without cross-asset return covariances.

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTLoss-versus-Rebalancing (LVR) is the dominant adverse-selection cost borne by liquidity providers on automated market makers. Under geometric Brownian motion, arbitrage profit scales with the probability of a profitable block, which vanishes as the block time $Δt \to 0$; this is the standing argument for ever-shorter blocks. Modeling the reference price instead as a jump-diffusion, I show that the constant-product LVR rate splits into a diffusion channel carrying the known multiplier $F(γ/(σ\sqrt{Δt}))$ and a jump channel $λV \cdot G(γ;m,δ^2)$ carrying no $Δt$, the two interacting only through an explicitly bounded remainder. The block schedule therefore governs only one channel. For symmetric jump laws the jump channel is moreover an exact lower bound, $\ell(Δt) \ge λV G > 0$, so the rate does not vanish as $Δt \to 0$, and descends slowly, as $\sqrt{Δt}$. At Ethereum's calibrated 12-second slot the rate is 471 bp/yr against a floor of 125, so only three quarters of LP loss is schedule-addressable. At Solana's 400 ms slot the jump channel already dominates. Netting the rate against per-block consensus cost, the LP-side optimal block time is invariant in pool size and in every jump parameter $(λ,m,δ)$: jumps shift the level of LP loss but not the planner's marginal tradeoff. Volatility, the fee tier, and consensus cost set the optimum, near 8 s. However, LVR is only one input to block-time welfare, so this bounds the LP-side contribution rather than settling the design question.

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTStock-level information produced by many active managers can aggregate into a public signal about the overall market. We show that daily return spreads between stocks with high and low active-manager ownership forecast next-day S&P 500 futures and ETF returns; market-timing strategies based on these spreads earn Sharpe ratios near one. Predictability concentrates among hedge funds and highly active mutual funds, strengthens in recessions and high-uncertainty states, exhibits no reversals, persists longer in tight-funding periods, and extends to global markets. A rational-expectations theory of specialized managers and slow-moving capital reconciles these findings and delivers new mechanisms of information aggregation. Structural estimation implies that market-wide information accounts for about 20% of model-implied stock-level signal variation among stocks heavily owned by active managers.

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTThis paper separates two claims conflated in the style-investing literature: that a firm's growth/value direction predicts risk, and that its extremity-distance from the ambiguous midpoint-predicts risk incrementally to direction. In a survivorship-free, point-in-time panel of 6,546 U.S. common stocks (market cap ≥ $300 million, 2004-2025, 196,438 firm-quarters), we run a horse race between the signed rank and its own extremity transform on three independent constructions. On price-to-sales, extremity is the whole story: direction is null (t =-0.25) while extremity survives fully intact (t = 9.7)-a genuine, if economically modest (0.050 SD), effect and our cleanest identification. On price, both terms survive jointly (direction t =-4.2, extremity t = 14.2), reported only as an upper bound given disclosed mechanical volatility content. On book-to-market the pattern inverts entirely: extremity collapses to zero (t = 0.43) once direction is included, while direction stays large (t = 17.2)-what looked like extremity is the familiar growth-options finding that low-book-to-market firms are more volatile (Cao, Simin, and Zhao 2008), not a distance-from-median effect. A battery of six placebo extremity transforms from characteristics unrelated to valuation (size, beta, bookto-market, momentum, MAX, idiosyncratic skewness) shows this symmetric pattern is not unique to valuation-all six predict forward idiosyncratic volatility, two more strongly than price-to-sales extremity itself-yet price-to-sales extremity survives every pairwise and joint test against them (t = 8.2 jointly, a 15% attenuation from its solo t = 9.9): a genuine incremental fact, not a newly documented class of risk determinant. Economic value concentrates in the price-based measure, which improves out-of-sample volatility forecasts against HAR-RV and EGARCH benchmarks (Clark-West t ≥ 3.4) and lowers realized portfolio volatility in 18 of 18 sample years, surviving a correlation-matched synthetic placebo. The identifying price-to-sales measure adds far less out-of-sample value and no portfolio benefit, and there is no return premium to either (t = 0.7): style extremity is a risk characteristic, not a return anomaly.

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTThe CAPM treats market beta as a sufficient statistic for priced aggregate risk. Yet expected returns compensate covariance with the stochastic discount factor, not covariance with the market itself. This distinction matters when some market fluctuations are orthogonal to the stochastic discount factor: they contribute to market volatility but not to the market risk premium. Market beta measures how much an asset covaries with the market, but not whether that covariance is generated by fluctuations relevant for marginal utility. I show that market beta combines exposure to priced and unpriced market variation. Under a priced-market spanning restriction, expected returns depend on priced beta, while unpriced beta has a zero structural price. Conventional beta therefore becomes an imperfect measure of compensated risk when assets load differently on the two components, generating CAPM pricing errors that increase with the difference in exposures. Empirically, priced and unpriced betas differ substantially across stocks. Consistent with the model, priced beta predicts average returns, unpriced beta carries little independent premium, and CAPM pricing errors increase with the exposure gap. Market beta's pricing performance therefore depends on what moves the market.
