integro-differential equationmaster equationKramers-Moyal expansionPawula theoremjump processesBoltzmann collision integral
ORIGINAL ABSTRACTThis paper argues, and demonstrates constructively, that the natural mathematical object describing a stochastic process is an integro-differential equation rather than a partial differential equation. We begin from the elementary random walk, reconstructed as a sequence of additions of random variables, and show that the integral operator is present in the very first step of the derivation: it is not introduced as a technique, an approximation, or a generalization, but arises directly from the requirement that probability be conserved over all possible antecedents of a state. Passing to continuous time yields the master equation, which is local in time and nonlocal in space. We then reconstruct, step by step, the route by which the familiar partial differential equations of the field are obtained from it: the Kramers-Moyal expansion converts the integral operator into a differential operator of infinite order, and truncation at second order produces the Fokker-Planck equation and, in the financial setting, the Black-Scholes equation. We identify precisely the condition under which this truncation is exact, namely the vanishing of all jump moments above the second, which is equivalent to the continuity of sample paths. We then recall Pawula's theorem, which states that the expansion may terminate after the second term or must contain infinitely many terms, so that no intermediate truncation preserves the positivity of the probability density. This closes the space of possibilities: a stochastic process is described either by a second-order partial differential equation, at the price of assuming continuous paths, or by the full integral operator. We illustrate the theorem numerically for a compound Poisson process, exhibiting explicitly the negative density produced by third-order truncation. A second and independent source of integral operators is then developed: whenever a quantity is a function of random variables, its density is obtained through a generalized functional built on the Dirac delta, as introduced in The Boltzmann Equation in Finance [2]. Sums, products and ratios all generate integral operators, and contingent claims generate probability atoms that no diffusion operator can produce from smooth data. Allowing the population to act as its own environment renders the operator quadratic and yields the Boltzmann collision integral, within which diffusive spreading and concentration coexist, admitting non-trivial steady states unavailable to a translation-invariant Fokker-Planck equation. We close by distinguishing integration over state space, which produces jumps, from integration over time, which produces memory.

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTContractual lock-ups make previously restricted shares eligible to trade on dates fixed months in advance. This paper asks whether the trading response to a Hong Kong IPO cornerstone release depends on other releases reaching the market on the same session. Congestion is formed from a frozen pre-outcome census of 504 eligible release events; the focal sample contains 226 complete event windows for 2022-2025 listing cohorts. The primary equal-event specification models log(1 + event-session volume relative to the preceding-20-session mean), retains 11 zero-volume sessions, and controls for market turnover, issuer size, and pre-event liquidity. The crowded-session coefficient is 0.432 (event-session clustered p = 0.010) and its interaction with log(1 + release strength) is-0.683 (p = 0.018). Event-week clustering, wildcluster bootstrap inference, month-constrained calendar randomization, alternative same-session congestion measures, placebo dates, and joint omission of the most crowded sessions support the negative interaction. The result is scale-sensitive: asinh and positive-only log outcomes agree, but an untransformed volume-ratio model and a Poisson pseudo-maximum-likelihood share-flow model do not. Holm adjustment across volume, return, and volatility interactions gives p = 0.054; neither price nor range volatility is robust. The evidence therefore describes a typical-event transformed-volume pattern, strongest among smaller releases. It does not establish aggregate share-flow pressure, price dislocation, or a causal market-capacity mechanism.

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTDo repeated IPO intermediaries exhibit stable contracting histories, and do those histories improve genuine out-of-time prediction? Sponsor histories use only strictly earlier listing dates. At the primary five-prior-deal threshold, the team adoption score has a raw AUC of 0.621 (year-stratified 95% bootstrap interval [0.571, 0.668]; within-year permutation p = 0.0004), while sponsor rankings persist across chronological halves (Spearman ρ = 0.610, p < 0.001). The controlled linear-probability coefficient is 0.390. Its p-value is 0.016 with leadsponsor clustered inference but 0.068 under a 4,999-draw wild-cluster bootstrap. Among single-sponsor IPOs the coefficient is 0.298 (clustered p = 0.081; wild-bootstrap p = 0.147), and omitting CICC reduces the full-team coefficient to 0.263 (p = 0.114). Expanding-window forecasts provide no stable incremental advantage: adding sponsor history changes pooled AUC from 0.691 to 0.682 (difference-0.009; bootstrap interval [-0.035, 0.017]). The difference is +0.030 in 2020-2023 but-0.040 in 2024-2026; the formal history-by-post-2024 interaction is imprecise (p = 0.660). Histories also do not predict release intensity or multi-tranche structure. Sponsor histories are persistent descriptors, but their association is dependence-sensitive and their predictive content becomes redundant as cornerstone adoption diffuses. The evidence is consistent with matching, networks, or routines rather than an exogenous sponsor effect or a portable forecasting advantage.

optimal executiontransient impactnonlinear impactperturbation theorypropagator modelfrontloading
ORIGINAL ABSTRACTWe study optimal execution with transient market impact when the instantaneous impact law is a weakly nonlinear deformation of the linear model, using rigorous perturbation theory. For completely monotone propagators with slippage, we show that the linear-impact optimizer has strictly positive trading rate, strengthening the nonnegativity result of Schied and Strehle (2021), and providing a necessary building block for rigorous perturbative expansions. We then consider a smooth deformation f (v; ε) of the instantaneous impact function, which reduces to linear impact at ε = 0, and develop a perturbative expansion in powers of ε. The expansion is asymptotic for smooth deformations and convergent for analytic deformations. The expansion is shown to be useful both for proving theorems, and also as a numerical tool. For propagators given by finite sums of exponentials, we prove in the weakly nonlinear regime the execution asymmetry that Curato, Gatheral, and Lillo (2017) observed numerically, and pointwise frontloading in the single exponential case. We also give a numerical example in which the square-root target is beyond the estimated radius of convergence, but the computed perturbation coefficients are still useful: ninth order truncation reduces the error of the linear baseline by a factor of about 43.

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTIn financial markets, a sequential policy that reacts systematically to price movements may become predictable to other market participants. This paper studies whether large language model (LLM) agents exhibit such directional structure through RetailAgent, an experimental framework in which an LLM observes anonymized intraday equity price histories and permitted state, then repeatedly chooses long (hold the stock) or flat (stay out) before the subsequent interval return is revealed. We compare returns during long and flat intervals along the same stock's intraday path after removing the overall fraction of long decisions. This exposure-matched measure reveals persistent negative timing across modality, horizon, state, and model family. Shuffling saved action sequences substantially attenuates the effect, showing that alignment between actions and subsequent returns drives the negative score. Feeding self-authored memories into decisions further increases policy persistence, while timing becomes more negative among stock-days on which the agent uses both actions. These results reveal stable, recoverable directional structure in sequential LLM financial decisions and a behavioral signal for studying how another participant could respond to a predictable policy.

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTHow markets perceive risk in announced M&A is difficult to measure, yet these perceptions are central to bidder valuation and deal outcomes. We address this problem using the Q&A sections of 3,465 M&A announcement conference calls. Analysts' questions are promising because they reveal the transaction-specific concerns that remain after management presents the deal. Using generative AI, we interpret these questions in context and construct a deal-level measure of analyst risk perception (ARP). ARP is higher in more uncertain and complex deals, predicts poorer completion outcomes and lower bidder valuation, and identifies when top-tier advisors add value: bidder gains are higher with top-tier advisors when ARP is high, but not when perceived risk is low. ARP also adds information beyond dictionary-based risk indices and pretrained financial-sentiment measures, showing that contextual analysis of analyst questions captures deal-specific risk signals missed by conventional text methods.

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTThis paper examines whether pre-shock bank balance-sheet characteristics explain differences in marketassessed resilience across five systemic shocks: COVID-19, the Russia-Ukraine invasion, the June 2022 inflation and monetary-tightening repricing, the Silicon Valley Bank (SVB) turmoil, and the April 2025 U.S. tariff repricing. The sample contains 172 listed banks from 19 major economies. Resilience is measured by cumulative abnormal returns from a country-market model, with separate impact and recovery windows. Cross-sectional regressions use pre-event bank fundamentals selected from 53 candidate variables through cross-validated LASSO and multicollinearity screening, followed by post-selection OLS with country fixed effects and country-clustered standard errors. The evidence is heterogeneous but economically interpretable. Impact windows place greater weight on funding usability, liability structure, and income mix; recovery windows more often reward conventional liquidity, direct equity, recognised loss absorption, and earnings rebuilding. Net interest margin is regime dependent, turning positive during the June 2022 repricing but negative during the COVID-19 impact window and the war recovery window. Broad risk-weighted capital is less stable than higher-quality or more direct equity measures in acute stress. The results are associative, not causal, and conventional significance levels should be read cautiously because the models are selected from the same data and inference relies on 19 country clusters.

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTA fund can look greener without its manager shifting the portfolio toward greener firms. Independent measures agree that U.S. mutual fund carbon intensity fell by more than a third, yet portfolio reweighting explains only 1.2 percent. Most of the decline instead comes from changing issuer emissions, sales denominators, estimates, and coverage. These inputs reverse the institutional sector trend and reshuffle manager rankings. Attribution replaces two in five managers selected for a green mandate. The replacements subsequently trade greener than those they displace. Carbon scores measure portfolio exposure; attribution reveals who deserves credit for changing it.

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTPassive inflows do not make firms issue equity indiscriminately. They redirect corporate share supply toward firms with real opportunities. I isolate those opportunities using federal purchasing growth in markets served by a firm's customers, which raises the firm's own sales. ORIGINAL ABSTRACTWe develop a simple and replicable five-variable model that identifies index-based investors with 98% accuracy. Our analysis shows that index ownership grew from 3.0% of global market capitalization in 2004 to 16.9% by 2023, driven by growth in explicit indexing. By the end of 2023, index-based investors own 10 percent or more of 5,300 firms globally. In the U.S., mid-caps have more index ownership than large-caps. In Asia and Europe, index ownership increases with firm size, and only the largest firms experience significant index ownership. Differences in market capitalization and free float help explain regional variations in index ownership.

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTInstitutional site visits enable investors to obtain incremental information beyond routine public disclosures and engage directly with corporate managers. This study posits that site visits may facilitate the early transmission of event-related information to the market, thereby contributing to price reactions before major corporate announcements. Using mandatory disclosures of site visits in China, this study finds that firms receiving site visits experience higher cumulative abnormal returns before profit distribution announcements, consistent with the view that site visits transmit information to the market before formal disclosure. The incremental pricing effect of site visits, however, weakens when event signals become stronger. Investor attention further facilitates the pricing of site-visit-related information, whereas different sources of information complexity either strengthen this pricing role in high-signal payout events or weaken the general transmission of site-visit information. Further trading evidence shows that major shareholders and executives are more likely to reduce their holdings when their trading operations are preceded by high-signal payout events with prior site visits, and that mutual funds affiliated with the corresponding site-visit institutions exhibit staged holding adjustments around these events. Overall, the evidence suggests that site visits provide an observable channel through which incremental information enters prices before formal disclosure, although this pricing role varies with event signal strength and information-processing conditions.

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTWhen an AI system appears to generate equity alpha, five explanations compete with genuine skill: factor exposure, a weak benchmark, data leakage, model complexity, and an advantage a conventional system could replicate. We test all five on the same signal. Using the peer-reviewed replication of 212 published anomalies, language-model and agentic arms forecast which anomalies persist after their original samples end. The arms earn significant factor alpha-and none of it survives comparison with a passive portfolio of all published anomalies, which requires no model at all. Leakage does not explain the result: contamination made performance worse. The models' verbal mechanism judgements outperform their own numeric scores, but in-sample persistence absorbs them. A composite forecast scoring 0.400 owes 98.5% of that to a statistic we supplied. Apparent AI alpha here is a benchmarking artefact, not information.

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTThis study analyses whether gold acts as a hedge or safe haven for the Indian stock market using long-run and crisis-specific return-based methods. Monthly data from 2008–2025 and daily data for the Global Financial Crisis, COVID-19, and the Russia–Ukraine war are used to estimate Pearson and Spearman correlations between gold and Nifty returns, with 60, 120, and 240-day windows. ORIGINAL ABSTRACTWe provide novel evidence on how investor attention interacts with corporate disclosure during the “full-consignment” shift in cross-border e-commerce, a reversal of the decade-long platform migration toward agency selling. Using 41,236 question-and-answer dialogues from China’s regulated investor interaction platforms for 118 listed supply-chain firms over 2022–2024, we document three counterintuitive findings. Consignment-related Q&A spikes generate overpricing that is larger and reverses faster than that associated with unregulated attention proxies: a five-day abnormal return of +2.9% fully reverses within six weeks, consistent with a credibility illusion created by exchange supervision. Attention also runs backward—investor questioning induces consignment narratives, concentrated in firms that never report consignment revenue. Finally, the market rewards narrative adopters while underreacting to genuine converters. The price-formation benefits of regulated interaction platforms are thus topic-contingent, and investor questioning constitutes a novel demand-side trigger of catering disclosure.​

We state it as a time-invariant mechanism driven by an unobserved latent state, and show that it leaves a researcher five constants to declare --- the recurrence bound $Lambda$ at a block length $b$, the invariance defect $epsilon_0$ of the representation it is declared of, the coherence times $ell_i$ of the state's coordinates, the signal ceiling $rho$ and the fraction $kappa$ of it contingent on the regime --- after which the architecture of a correct quantitative investment system is nearly forced.

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTQuantum illumination has been proposed as a theoretical route to detecting low-reflectivity targets, such as stealth aircraft, in high-background-noise environments where classical radar performance degrades. The protocol, as originally formulated (Lloyd, 2008; Tan et al., 2008), uses continuous-variable entangled light (two-mode squeezed vacuum) and a specific phase-sensitive joint receiver to achieve a theoretical detection advantage over classical illumination of matched energy, even though the entanglement itself does not survive the round trip through a lossy, noisy channel. This study investigates whether that advantage appears in a simpler, discrete-variable (qubit) toy model, of the kind commonly used for pedagogical intuition, implemented on PKTron and cross-checked on IBM Quantum hardware. A rigorously fair comparison was constructed in which an entangled Bell pair and a classically correlated (separable) mixture of matched initial correlation strength were each subjected to identical loss and background-noise channels, with detection performance assessed via the same joint correlation measurement (Z⊗ Z expectation) in both cases. In PKTron simulation, the entangled probe showed a correlation separation between target-present and target-absent hypotheses of 0.0100 at zero background noise, decreasing to 0.0025 at high background noise, while the classically correlated probe showed a substantially larger separation, decreasing from 0.1000 to 0.0500 over the same range-indicating no entanglement advantage, and if anything, a disadvantage, in this discrete model. This qualitative finding was independently corroborated on IBM Quantum's ibm_kingston hardware, using natural qubit T1 relaxation (rather than an artificially injected noise parameter) as the loss channel: entangled correlation degraded to 54.5% of its initial value after 60 microseconds, compared to 77.7% retained by the classically correlated mixture over the same interval. These results indicate that the theoretical quantum illumination advantage does not straightforwardly emerge from a simple discrete-qubit correlation model, consistent with the broader understanding that the effect is specific to continuousvariable Gaussian states and phase-sensitive joint detection, and consistent with quantum illumination's status as a theoretical concept with no demonstrated range or signal-to-noise advantage over classical radar to date.

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTOn declared supports containing a one-parameter family of terminal-segment curve deformations, and under the printed integrability and quote-Slater hypotheses, no finite book of caplets, floorlets, physical or cash-settled swaptions, or standard-timing CMS products on any finite strike-tenor panel bounds any superlinear moment of the annuity pricing weight: exact joint caplet-swaption calibration fails an observable well-posedness criterion. One payment-timing quote per date repairs this. The in-advance claim's price is affinely a second moment of the inverse terminal bond price, yielding a market-implied coercive gauge, a compact closed weighted-smile image, and an exact support-function dual; a single settlement family on the compounded tape carries every date's budget, while plain compounded futures provably cannot. Deterministic fixtures certify each mechanism.

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTIn 2026, U.S. options markets went through three changes at roughly the same time: FINRA eliminated the Pattern Day Trader (PDT) rule and its $25,000 minimum-equity threshold (effective June 4, 2026); zero-daysto-expiration (0DTE) options kept growing, reaching a record 66.2% of S&P 500 index options volume by July; and Cboe completed a near-24-hour trading window covering SPX, VIX, Mini-SPX, and Russell 2000 index options. Using Cboe's own investor disclosures, this paper documents that all three changes are described to investors primarily in terms of engagement and volume growth, while retail-facing communications about the same events emphasize flexibility and access. This paper does not claim that any entity intended to harm retail traders, nor does it establish a causal link between these friction removals and retail trading losses. What it documents is an observable asymmetry in how the commercial value of these changes is communicated to different audiences. Combined with well-established findings that most retail options buyers lose money and that traders routinely fail to exit at planned loss levels, this asymmetry points to a gap in current disclosure regimes. The paper proposes a voluntary, opt-in risk control feature-a platform-level button, available inside any retail trading app, that traders can turn on or off at will-which, once activated, locks a trader's selfdefined loss threshold in place for a set period. Rooted in behavioral-economics commitment-device theory, it holds traders to their own stated risk plan at the moment when research predicts they are most likely to abandon it. AI is proposed as implementation infrastructure for this feature, not as the theoretical contribution.

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTBolivia possesses approximately 22% of identified global lithium resources-one of the world's largest endowments-yet in 2025 produced just 2,400 tonnes of lithium carbonate equivalent, less than 1% of South American output. This paper demonstrates that Bolivia's production gap is primarily institutional: a bilateral monopoly with Chinese and Russian state-owned enterprises has trapped the sovereign in a low-BATNA equilibrium, enabling counterparties to capture quasi-rents through opaque pricing and one-sided risk allocation. We propose Commodity-Linked Participation Rights (CLPRs), an exchange-cleared security that transforms Bolivia's bargaining structure from bilateral negotiation to a "negotiauction"-a hybrid mechanism in which competitive bidding determines price while negotiated governance provisions preserve sovereign discretion. Drawing on Subramanian's negotiauction theory and Acemoglu and Robinson's institutional economics framework, we develop a formal bargaining model in which the credible availability of a CLPR auction improves the sovereign's outside option, altering the equilibrium terms of bilateral resource negotiations. Under our baseline parameterisation, the simulated effective financing cost falls from an implicit 12%+ to approximately 7.4%, with the probability of payment distress declining from 35% to 8.2%. The framework generalises to other resource-rich developing economies facing sovereignty-financing trade-offs.

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTPower-plus valuation gives an elementary one-period option pricing formula and an explicit recursion under repeated application. We study when this algebraically prescribed recursion also admits a dynamically coherent multi-period martingale stopping representation. The key restriction is recursive. Whenever the holder continues at a successor state, that state must itself support the remaining prescribed recursion. For a stylized convertible claim, we solve this backward feasibility problem exactly. With n ≥ 2 future conversion dates, the viable states form the finite half-open interval D_n = [0, d_n), where d_n is the exact viability boundary. These boundaries contract strictly as the number of remaining conversion dates increases. Once finite exercise states disappear, recursive viability becomes strictly more restrictive than the ordinary one-step martingale bound. We construct finite-support Borel Markov kernels that realize the prescribed stopping values throughout the viable domains for each fixed contract. Finally, under dense conversion grids we identify a sharp phase transition. Depending on the relative scaling of the power parameter and the grid spacing, the issuance viability boundary either converges to a finite limit or diverges.

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTThis paper specifies a Layer-1 blockchain protocol whose monetary issuance is mechanically indexed to the network's verifiable operating cost plus a small, bounded margin. New tokens are minted only to the extent required to cover attested energy, compute, and infrastructure expenditure incurred in processing and finalizing blocks, and to fund a stability buffer. The design objective is a cryptoasset whose issuance adjusts to verified operating cost and prevailing token value, limiting cumulative dilution and dampening price volatility over time without reliance on fiat reserves. This revision incorporates a significant development in market infrastructure: the emergence of independent GPU rental-rate benchmarks and exchange-listed compute derivatives, which supply the protocol with regulated, market-settled reference rates for its cost oracle and permit hedging of the protocol's cost base. We present the issuance rule, admissible cost basis, attestation architecture, oracle design, fee and buffer mechanics, consensus model, threat model, governance, and institutional use cases for real-world-asset (RWA) tokenization and settlement.

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTNo technology has ever moved so much capital in so little time: the four large cloud groups plan to invest around USD 735 billion in 2026 — more than five times their 2023 outlay —, NVIDIA's data-centre business approaches USD 200 billion in annual revenue, and the model providers OpenAI and Anthropic report annualised revenues of more than 40 and 65 billion US dollars respectively. This paper — the second of six on the great megatrends — classifies artificial intelligence as a general purpose technology, maps its value chain from chips through data centres and models to applications, and tests the bubble question against hard numbers. The empirical picture cuts both ways. On the one hand, controlled studies document sizeable productivity gains — 15 per cent in customer service, 40 per cent time saved in writing tasks, 56 per cent faster programming — and the investments are largely paid out of the current profits of the world's most profitable companies. On the other hand, index concentration has reached historic highs — the ten largest US names make up more than 40 per cent of the S&P 500, more than at the peak of the dotcom bubble —, circular financing between chip makers, cloud providers and model firms is growing, and according to a widely discussed MIT study 95 per cent of corporate pilot projects have yet to deliver a measurable profit contribution. For investors, the paper names listed companies along the entire chain — exclusively large and mid caps, with business idea and trading venues — and applies the fixed ETF checklist: physical replication, fund size of at least EUR 0.2 billion, sustainability classification, costs, the currency question, issuer, UCITS framework and exchange trading. The most important single lesson: whoever holds a world index already owns roughly a third of the AI complex through its heavyweights — every additional position is a deliberate overweight and should be sized accordingly.

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTFirms create value by acquiring workers who complement their productive needs, yet early applicant screening may impede this process by excluding potentially productive candidates before firms observe richer information about their qualifications and fit. We study how this friction affects firm value using staggered Ban-the-Box laws, which delay criminal-history screens until later in the hiring process. Following adoption, affected firms experience higher valuations, especially where an expanded applicant pool should be more consequential. Firms also fill vacancies faster, report fewer labor shortages, and experience fewer early worker separations. These improvements in labor acquisition are followed by higher productivity, profitability, and cash flow, while volatility, default risk, and the implied cost of equity decline. Our findings identify early applicant screening as an important labor-market friction and suggest that reducing screening-related barriers to labor acquisition can increase firm value through both cash-flow and discount-rate channels.

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTBy 2050, the United Nations projects that just over two-thirds of the world's population will live in cities — with almost one billion urban dwellers added along the way. This paper — the third of six on the great megatrends — places urbanisation in its economic context: from the agglomeration advantages that make cities more productive than their hinterland, through the housing shortage of the rich world, to the infrastructure gap that consultancies put at more than 100 trillion US dollars through 2040. The paper covers six fields of action of the megatrend: densification and intelligent housing, the green and resilient city, smart cities and digital connectivity, new urban mobility, the demographic change of the ageing city, and the tension between growing metropolises and shrinking regions. Empirically, a twofold picture emerges: the large cities of the rich world face historic scarcity — Germany alone is short of roughly 1.4 million homes and vacancy in its metropolises is close to zero — while at the same time half of Europe's municipalities are shrinking and a third of the world's shrinking cities are in China. ORIGINAL ABSTRACTThe English Devolution and Community Empowerment Act 2026 provides for the removal of upward-only rent review (UORR) protection from variable rent reviews in most new and renewed business tenancies in England and Wales once Schedule 7A commences. This paper develops an ex-ante, state-contingent valuation framework to quantify the contractual income protection removed. A Monte Carlo expected-cash-flow model compares upward-only and two-way review rules on identical simulated rent paths, using published contemporary market evidence on growth, yields and lease structure, with volatility and rent-process sensitivities. For affected at-market tenyear leases, the geometric Brownian motion (GBM) capital-value effects are 0.47% for lower-risk logistics, 1.19% for prime offices and 3.91% for a weak-growth secondary-office scenario. Their asset-yield equivalents are 6.3, 15.7 and 65.2 basis points. Larger estimates arise in protected legacy stock and adverse contractual states: 6.85% for a legacy 25-year lease and 8.26% for an over-rented retail scenario under full enforcement. In the over-rented retail scenario, 78.46% of fully enforceable value is concentrated where protected rent exceeds 1.60 times the corresponding twoway rent. An illustrative moneyness-dependent realisability stress lowers the over-rented retail scenario estimate to 3.88% under GBM and 4.30% under trend mean reversion. Among modelled leases exposed to at least one review, initial rent state and the number of review opportunities are more informative about UORR value than property sector alone, while cash-flow duration causes capital-value and yield-equivalent rankings to diverge. ORIGINAL ABSTRACTThe verdict paper (Sun, 2026e) established four claims of the VVIX-temperature program survive: the sign of the thermal Kramers law, the priced NEI state variable, and a striking unexamined fact, two independent operationalizations of market temperature, a Boltzmann VIX microstructure-implied temperature Tc and a VVIX-based kinetic temperature Tk, correlate at 0.8277 (0.8288 in trading hours, 0.8286 in event time) while differing radically in observability: Tc is measurable only when the Boltzmann VIX microstructure fit gate is valid (38.4% of trading hours), whereas Tk is continuous. This paper promotes that fact to theory. We model the VIX microstructure field as coupled to two weakly coupled heat baths, the direct analogue of the two-temperature electron-phonon systems of laser physics, with coupling validated by the measured 0.8277, and we show that (i) the unification ceiling observed in Paper V (corr(G, Gfield) = 0.6718 ≤ corr(Tc, Tk) = 0.8277) is a structural consequence of two-thermometer statistics; (ii) the thermometer coverage k(t), the fraction of time the curve carries identifiable critical dynamics, is not a nuisance but an order parameter for the single-mode absorbing state identified in Paper V; (iii) the live regime (T*B = -0.0009, VVIX* = 142.94, ΔU = 5.7106) is exactly the flat-barrier state the theory predicts under thermometer divergence. We derive five falsifiable predictions (Q1-Q5), pre-register their evaluation thresholds for the next twelve months of live data, and specify the kill conditions under which the dual-temperature theory joins P1 and P4 in the refuted column.

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTThis study examines how China's Medium-Term Lending Facility (MLF) transmits to financial asset prices, focusing on asymmetric responses in bond and stock markets. Using monthly data from September 2014 to May 2025, we analyze changes in the outstanding balance of the MLF together with one-year government bond yield changes, the term spread, credit spread changes, and Shanghai Composite Index returns. A vector autoregression model is used to estimate average dynamic relationships, while a time-varying parameter VAR with stochastic volatility captures changes in transmission across market regimes. The results show that MLF shocks are transmitted most directly through the government bond market. An expansion in MLF liquidity generally lowers the one-year government bond yield and affects the term spread mainly through short-rate movements. By contrast, credit spreads respond weakly and briefly, and stock returns show only a short-lived positive reaction. Time-varying estimates confirm that the bond-market channel is more stable than the credit-spread or stock-market channels, although the strength of transmission differs during periods such as the 2015 stock market turbulence, the COVID-19 shock, and the post-pandemic policy transition. These findings suggest that the MLF affects financial asset prices primarily through the government bond yield structure, while its effects on credit spreads and stock returns are weaker, less direct, and less persistent.

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTAdaptive liquidity systems may have identical observable composition while differing in the redistributions that are feasible from their current states. This paper develops a constructive minimal model to examine when a mathematical representation of redistribution capability is dynamically sufficient for a specified problem. The model contains reserve, working, buffer, and strategic liquidity components and compares alternative redistribution architectures from a common initial state. Three results are established. First, a scalar aggregation of immediately admissible transfer capacity is dynamically insufficient for an urgent one-step liquidity-shock problem because it can identify systems with different immediate response capabilities. Second, a weighted directed graph is dynamically sufficient for a restricted two-step thresholdreachability problem when the initial state and transition rules are fixed across the system class, because it preserves the channel directions, nominal capacities, and path structure required to determine the relevant response. Third, the same graph representation becomes insufficient when systems with different transition operators are admitted. Two systems with identical initial states, admissible nominal actions, and weighted graphs may produce different one-step responses when the effective contribution of a transfer depends on its transition mechanism. In that context, an operator-based representation is dynamically sufficient. The construction distinguishes nominal channel capacity, immediately admissible transfer capacity, and effective dynamic contribution, and shows how information discarded by a representation may become dynamically relevant. The results demonstrate that no scalar, graph, or operator representation is universally adequate. A representation is dynamically sufficient only when it preserves the distinctions that determine the relevant future response for the specified system class, time horizon, and dynamic context. The paper therefore provides a constructive illustration of task-relative dynamic sufficiency within adaptive liquidity systems and Wave Liquidity Redistribution Theory (WLRT).

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTThis paper asks whether stock markets predict the economy or shape it. Markets called the 2009 and 2020 recoveries before data confirmed them, which looks like strong evidence for market efficiency. ORIGINAL ABSTRACTLong shot innovation projects, including fundamental research, are persistently underfunded because they combine long investment horizons with low probabilities of success and highly skewed, often binary, payoff distributions. Financial engineering theory suggests that pooling such projects and allocating cash flows across tranches that differ in seniority can transform these uncertain outcomes into more conventional risk-return profiles. While the existing literature has focused almost exclusively on the potential of such structures for institutional investors, this article examines their eligibility for European retail investors operating under the current investor protection regime. We show that retail eligibility depends on a non-linear interaction between regulatory risk classifications, the allocation of success across tranches, and the degree of diversification within the underlying research portfolio. Carefully designed portfolio and tranche structures can satisfy retail eligibility requirements while preserving exposure to innovation related upside potential, also when including mandatory liquidity reserves and representative fees. Building on these findings, we outline a governance framework for a dedicated funding vehicle capable of managing the resulting asset and liability structure. Mobilising household savings to finance research and innovation complements existing public funding instruments and contributes to the objectives of the European Savings and Investments Union.

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTWe examine China’s split share reform, a setting where controlling shareholders compensated minority tradable shareholders to convert nontradable shares into tradable ones. We find that controlling shareholders minimized total compensation by transferring private benefits—proxied by abnormal perk expenses—to a subset of tradable shareholders in exchange for their support of low-compensation plans. These private benefit transfers were more prevalent in firms with strong incentives to complete the reform expeditiously, those facing difficult negotiations, and those with weaker corporate governance. Furthermore, nontradable shareholders were strategic in their targeting: they utilized these transfers more aggressively in firms that subsequently exhibited significant operating improvements and superior stock returns.

open innovationabsorptive capacityjoint venturesemerging marketsexport capabilityprocess tracing
ORIGINAL ABSTRACTEmerging-market joint ventures (JVs) frequently rely on foreign technology to navigate institutional voids-regulatory ambiguity, fragmented supply chains, and infrastructure deficits-yet many struggle to convert this knowledge into global export capability. Prior research typically models foreign technology licencing, internal R&D, and external search as discrete, additive inputs; we instead conceptualise them as an interdependent configuration. We ask how JVs recombine these heterogeneous knowledge sources to build export capability under resource scarcity. Using an abductive, longitudinal process-tracing design across ten legal entities in eight Indian manufacturing and life-science contexts (FY2015-FY2025), we prioritise audited statutory and regulatory disclosures to mitigate self-reporting bias. We find that successful JVs follow a sequential process-then-product pathway whose ordering is dictated by resource scarcity. We refine absorptive capacity theory by showing that realised absorptive capacity functions as a threshold condition rather than a continuous, linear moderator. Below this critical capability floor, foreign licencing deepens technological dependence; above it, JVs configure inbound open innovation as an active institutional buffer, transforming domestic compliance constraints into scalable export capabilities. Export readiness thus depends less on the raw volume of innovation inputs than on the architectural alignment of local R&D and technical governance.

change of numéraireWasserstein stabilityuniform integrabilityannuity measuremartingale optimal transportself-normalized importance sampling
ORIGINAL ABSTRACTReweighting a probability law by a positive numéraire and pushing forward the payoffto-numéraire ratio yields the change-of-numéraire reweighting: the swap-rate law under the annuity measure, the numéraire-inversion involution of martingale optimal transport, and the population form of self-normalized importance sampling. We characterize exactly when it is Wasserstein-stable. Along weakly convergent inputs with uniformly integrable numéraires and a strictly positive limiting numéraire mean, convergence of the reweighted laws is equivalent to a uniform integrability condition, computed under the inputs, on one explicit family in the payoff and numéraire. At first order the numéraire cancels, the sole obstruction being payoff mass where the numéraire vanishes; absent such mass, prices and first moments pass to the limit under a uniformly integrable payoff alone, with no assumption on the reciprocal numéraire. Two-atom examples with bounded inputs attain the threshold exactly. Applications characterize a standing moment assumption in the transport literature and delimit which annuity-measure statistics survive.

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTOn declared supports containing a one-parameter family of terminal-segment curve deformations, and under the printed integrability and quote-Slater hypotheses, no finite book of caplets, floorlets, physical or cash-settled swaptions, or standard-timing CMS products on any finite strike-tenor panel bounds any superlinear moment of the annuity pricing weight: exact joint caplet-swaption calibration fails an observable well-posedness criterion. One payment-timing quote per date repairs this. The in-advance claim's price is affinely a second moment of the inverse terminal bond price, yielding a market-implied coercive gauge, a compact closed weighted-smile image, and an exact support-function dual; a single settlement family on the compounded tape carries every date's budget, while plain compounded futures provably cannot. Deterministic fixtures certify each mechanism.

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTTransport is undergoing its greatest transformation since the horse carriage gave way to the motor car: in 2025 one in four new cars sold worldwide was electric, driverless taxis complete roughly half a million paid rides a week in American metropolitan areas, and software is turning the vehicle from a product of mechanical craftsmanship into a computer on wheels. This paper-the first of six devoted to the great megatrends-orders the field of future mobility along its five arenas: decarbonisation and alternative drive systems, autonomous driving, connectivity, shared mobility, and the urban transformation including micromobility. The paper examines market positions and timetables: battery prices have fallen by more than 90 per cent since 2010 (2025: USD 108 per kilowatt-hour), five-minute charging is series production reality in China, driverless lorries have been running in Texas since 2025, and the robotaxi market could grow to more than USD 400 billion by 2035 — while the privately owned Level 4 car is, by broad agreement, unlikely before the 2030s and will dominate the vehicle fleet only decades later. For investors, the paper names listed companies along the entire value chain — large and mid caps exclusively — with their business ideas and trading venues, and identifies two ETFs that pass the selection checklist developed in the text. The investment conclusion cuts both ways: the megatrend is real, but its returns are unevenly distributed and have historically flowed to the suppliers of scarce key technology rather than to the car brands. Thematic ETFs launched near peak sentiment have lost roughly 30 per cent in risk-adjusted terms over their first five years. Whoever wants to take part therefore diversifies across the value chain, weights platform and technology leaders above hopeful newcomers, avoids naming small specialists, and measures success in decades, not quarters.

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTThe allocation of saving and borrowing between banks and markets and the transmission of shocks through the financial system vary widely across countries and over time. While existing work emphasizes supply-side determinants such as institutions, regulation, and intermediary technology, we study a demand-side determinant: household and firm composition and their demand for imperfectly substitutable financial claims. We build and estimate an equilibrium model of financial intermediation that uses granular household and firm data to recover how financial demand varies with individual characteristics and aggregates across households and firms. Reaggregating over alternative populations changes equilibrium financial structure and shock transmission. Differences in household and firm composition explain nearly all the 1980-2019 decline in banks' share of U.S. private-sector saving and 69 percent of the cross-country variation, but less variation in banks' share of financing. Composition also alters the impact of an increase in Treasury supply by changing which sector absorbs the new debt: under the 1980 distribution of household and firm characteristics, banks absorb twice as much, raising their cost of lending and generating greater crowding out of private credit.

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTHow do residential real estate markets value large-scale climate policies? We study how Germany's coal phase-out affects residential property values near decommissioned coal-fired power plants. Combining detailed residential property listing data from 2007 to 2023 with the staggered timing of plant closures, we estimate dynamic spatial difference-in-differences (DiD) models that account for the geographic proximity. Nearby residential property values decline by 8.2%, implying aggregate homeowner wealth losses of approximately €1.9 billion. To distinguish economic from environmental adjustment, we examine changes in local employment, population, purchasing power, and local air pollution. Declines in population, employment and purchasing power coincide with falling residential property values, whereas improvements in air quality do not seem to offset these losses. Our findings show that residential real estate markets primarily capitalize the deterioration of local economic fundamentals rather than improvements in environmental quality, implying that climate policy generates substantial localized household wealth effects through residential real estate markets - a distributional channel that complements conventional evaluations focused on aggregate environmental benefits and macroeconomic adjustment.

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTBackground: Cryptocurrency is a digital decentralized currency that enables peer-to-peer transactions without the involvement of intermediaries, using blockchain technology to ensure security and transparency. These emotions can help understand when and what behavioral intentions toward cryptocurrency adoption are necessary. These insights contribute to the growing literature on fintech adoption in emerging economies and provide valuable guidance for policymakers and investors formulating cryptocurrency regulations in Nepal. Objectives: It aims to investigate the influence of perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, trust, and perceived risk constructs attached to an individual's intention to be involved in cryptocurrency transactions. It finally aims to study the relationships among these variables and their effect on cryptocurrency adoption in the Nepal context. Methods: The study uses a quantitative descriptive design and snowball sampling alone to extract information from cryptocurrency users in Nepal. A structured online questionnaire was used to gather 272 responses and analyzed using correlation and regression to investigate the significance of the proposed hypotheses. Results: Findings show that perceived usefulness, ease, or trust significantly and positively influence behavioral intention toward cryptocurrency adoption, while perceived risk harms adoption because users worry about market volatility, regulatory uncertainty, and security threats. Despite the government's legal restrictions, many Nepalese citizens are still involved in cryptocurrency transactions, seeing it as a source of financial benefit and investment opportunity. Conclusion: The study attests that perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, and trust motivate behavior toward adopting cryptocurrency, while perceived risk provides a barrier. This enlightens policymakers on balanced regulatory measures that address risks while encouraging innovation in digital finance. These findings would provide valuable implications for policymakers, financial institutions, and technology developers in outlining the future of cryptocurrency regulation and adoption strategies.

The analysis focuses on the economic relationship between Hyperliquid's protocol activity and HYPE through the Assistance Fund's open-market acquisition and permanent burn mechanism, while separating token utility from legal equity ownership. ORIGINAL ABSTRACTRedistribution capability is a structural component of adaptive liquidity systems, but its mathematical representation is not unique. A scalar quantity, reachable set, transition graph, transformation operator, or geometric object may preserve different information about the same underlying capability structure. This paper examines five principal mathematical realizations of redistribution capability: scalar, set-valued, graph-based, operator-based, and geometric. Relations between representations are formalized through an information preorder defined by deterministic recoverability. Mutual recoverability induces an equivalence relation, and the resulting equivalence classes form a partially ordered set under the induced information relation. The analysis distinguishes the underlying redistribution-capability structure Cσ(x) from a particular representation RA(σ, x) = ρA(Cσ(x)). For a specified class of dynamic contexts D, a dynamic response map ΨD is used to identify capability structures that are dynamically indistinguishable for the problem under consideration. The central result gives a necessary and sufficient factorization criterion for dynamic sufficiency. A representation ρ : C → Z is dynamically sufficient relative to D if and only if ΨD = Ψˆ︁ D ◦ ρ. Equivalently, every fiber of ρ must be contained within a single dynamic-equivalence class. This criterion separates generic information loss from dynamically relevant information loss. A representation may be non-injective and compress structural information while remaining dynamically sufficient, provided that it does not identify capability structures with different relevant dynamic responses. The resulting analysis provides a criterion for selecting mathematical realizations of redistribution capability relative to the system class, analytical task, and dynamic contexts under consideration. It does not assume a universal scalar realization or claim universal sufficiency of any single adaptive state representation.

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTThis article examines three structural crises that the nation-state confronts simultaneously in the twenty-first century: demographic ageing and the unsustainability of social security systems; labour-market transformation driven by automation and artificial intelligence; and climate-induced food insecurity and migration. Drawing on recent institutional and academic literature (2018-2026), the study argues that these crises are not merely concurrent but mutually reinforcing through feedback loops that generate a spiral, placing the classical nation-state / welfare-state model under a performance-legitimacy crisis. The article proposes a four-layer model of "regulatory stakeholder capitalism" that moves beyond voluntary stakeholder capitalism by incorporating a state-capacity filter, SME proportionality, regulatory-arbitrage safeguards, and an inter-stakeholder prioritisation mechanism. Prepared as a descriptive-critical literature review, the paper advances five testable hypotheses and outlines a three-stage research programme intended to ground future quantitative inquiry. The contribution lies in integrating demographic-fiscal, technological and climatic pressures into a single institutional-response framework that treats state capacity as a central filter rather than a residual variable.

This study develops rational expectation models to explore the market impacts of investors' asymmetrical acquisition of range information. ORIGINAL ABSTRACTThe United States has increasingly leveraged the Entity List as a key instrument within its export control regime. While existing studies primarily examine the political motivations and macroeconomic consequences of these measures, we extend the literature by empirically investigating the link between U.S. Entity List targeting Chinese entities and stock price crash risk of affected Chinese firms. ORIGINAL ABSTRACTInvestment banking, shadow banking, and high-frequency trading are among those manifestations of modern finance that evoke fascination and mistrust in equal measure. Drawing on the academic literature and on current data from international institutions (Financial Stability Board, ESMA, SEC, LSEG), this paper examines what these lines of business actually are, how they function, who conducts them, and whose interests they serve. The analysis shows that all of the activities examined constitute legal, economically well-founded, and in large part regulated businesses whose questionable reputation stems chiefly from opacity, conflicts of interest, and isolated excesses. Investment banking is a highly concentrated business of a few large banks, with worldwide fee income of $60.5 billion in the first half of 2025 alone. Shadow banking, as recorded by the Financial Stability Board, comprises assets of $256.8 trillion and thus already 51 per cent of the global financial system. In high-frequency trading, roughly 55 per cent of US and up to 43 per cent of European equity trading volume is attributable to strategies whose reaction times are measured in millionths of a second; the costs associated with latency arbitrage amount to roughly five billion dollars per year worldwide (Aquilina, Budish, and O'Neill, 2022). For investors, a differentiated assessment follows: none of the businesses examined is disreputable per se, and none is free of risk. Those who understand how they work, who the participants are, and where the profits originate can weigh opportunities and dangers realistically — and may, in selected cases, participate in these markets themselves, whether through listed trading firms or through regulated credit funds.

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTSatellite-to-ground quantum key distribution (QKD) has been proposed and experimentally demonstrated (e.g., China's Micius satellite) as a means of extending quantum-secured communication beyond fiber-optic range, with direct relevance to naval fleet communications and aircraft-to-base communications where mobile assets cannot rely on fixed fiber infrastructure. Unlike this research group's companion terrestrial BB84 study, which evaluated eavesdropper detection under near-ideal channel conditions, satellite links are dominated by a different physical effect: atmospheric photon loss, driven by slant-path absorption, scattering, beam divergence, and elevation-angle-dependent atmospheric thickness. This study models that effect using PKTron's density-matrix simulator, explicitly separating two physically distinct phenomena that are frequently conflated in simplified models: heralded photon loss (which reduces raw key rate without directly causing bit errors) and detector dark counts (a roughly constant background click rate that becomes proportionally significant, and increasingly drives quantum bit error rate, QBER, as the real signal weakens). Across four simulated transmittance scenarios representing satellite pass geometries from zenith (η=0.50) to near-horizon (η=0.005), sifted key count fell from 547 to 15 bits per 2,000 transmitted qubits, while QBER rose from 2.6% to 33.3%, driven by dark counts constituting an increasing fraction (1.3% to 60.0%) of all detector clicks. Hardware validation was performed on IBM Quantum's ibm_marrakesh processor for the surviving-photon measurement step, using the same classical channel model to determine which photons survived transmission. At η=0.50, hardware measurement yielded a 0.550 click rate (matching theoretical prediction) with 12 sifted bits and 0.000 QBER; at η=0.03, a larger sample (400 transmitted qubits) yielded a 0.037 click rate (again matching prediction) with 8 sifted bits and a QBER of 0.125, consistent with the simulated prediction of elevated error rates at low transmittance. These results confirm, in both simulation and on real quantum hardware, that atmospheric loss degrades satellite QKD primarily through reduced key rate and a distinct, gradual, dark-count-driven QBER increase-qualitatively different from the sharp, immediate QBER signature of eavesdropping demonstrated in this group's companion terrestrial QKD study-a distinction with direct relevance to link budget engineering for naval and airborne quantum-secured communication systems.

sovereign defaultequity returnsquantitative macro modelcapital accumulationevent study
ORIGINAL ABSTRACTThis paper evaluates the extent to which standard quantitative sovereign default models exhibit equity return responses around default risk spikes comparable to the data. It finds that they largely do not. Hébert and Schreger (2017) employ a high-frequency event study around legal rulings and report a 10% increase in default risk causes a 6% decline in firms’ market value. A workhorse sovereign default model augmented with capital accumulation delivers only a 0.2% equity value drop. Three features account for the disconnect: the absence of private capital outflows and trade surpluses during default, the model’s counterfactual prediction of rising dividends, and the nominal depreciation embedded in the dollar-denominated index used in the data.

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTOn August 10, 2026, Nvidia announced memoranda of understanding with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs, and KKR to mobilize over five hundred billion dollars of third-party capital through GPU-backed financing platforms. This paper argues that the structure introduces a category of risk that existing asset-backed securitisation theory does not formally address. I identify three conditions shared with the mortgage-backed securities market before 2008: correlated collateral values, unproven cash flow assumptions, and asymmetric incentives between originators and downstream debt holders. I then define two risk categories specific to technology asset-backed lending: Vendor-Circular Financing, which describes the structural conflict created when a manufacturer backstops credit facilities enabling purchases of its own products, and Innovation-Cycle Depreciation, which describes the systematic destruction of collateral value triggered by the vendor's own product roadmap. Secondary market data shows that H100 GPUs have lost approximately seventy-three percent of their 2023 value by mid-2026, providing preliminary empirical grounding for both risk categories.

ORIGINAL ABSTRACTFinancial technology has reshaped the way capital is raised, invested, traded, and supervised. Innovations in electronic trading, algorithmic execution, digital advisory services, and distributed infrastructure have altered the structure of capital markets and the delivery of investment management services, while introducing new categories of operational, technological, and regulatory risk. This research examines financial technology as it applies to investment management and capital market services. It considers the FinTech ecosystem and its participants, the digital transformation of primary and secondary markets, the risk management and cybersecurity implications of technology adoption, the governance and internal control frameworks required to oversee it, and the contribution of financial technology to financial inclusion. ORIGINAL ABSTRACTWe characterise minimum-distortion wealth taxation under two contrasting normative criteria within a Fokker-Planck framework on log-wealth: the JKO free-energy gap, an information-theoretic measure aligned with the Mirrleesian decision-distortion tradition, and the squared 2-Wasserstein distance from the no-tax distribution at horizon $T$, a transport-geometric measure aligned with the Saez-Zucman distributional-compression tradition. Restricting to the neutrality-preserving (C1)-(C3) schedule class of a companion paper (Froseth 2026), both optima admit closed forms in the two-dimensional design plane parametrised by the corporate-dividend retention $k = (1-τ_c)(1-τ_d)$ and the proportional wealth-tax rate $τ_w$. The JKO optimum partitions the regime axis into three phases as a function of the dimensionless ratio $ρ= Σ_0 m_0/σ^2$, with $m_0 = μ- σ^2/2$ the geometric mean log-return: a pure wealth-tax phase at low $ρ$, a mixed-instrument phase at intermediate $ρ$, and a pure flow-tax phase at high $ρ$. The $W_2$ optimum, by contrast, is degenerate in this calibration: it pins to the pure flow-tax corner across the whole regime axis. The criterion contrast admits an economically meaningful reading via a bluntness index $B(m_0) = b/(a m_0)$ that measures the wealth-tax channel's mean-displacement-per-revenue overshoot relative to the flow-tax channel; JKO weights $B$ linearly, $W_2$ weights it quadratically, and the two normative traditions correspond to this difference in weighting. Norwegian-flavoured calibrations sit inside the JKO mixed-instrument phase under stock-heavy portfolio volatility but move into the pure flow-tax phase under the realised effective volatility of typical real-estate-heavy households.

LLM 투자 조언이 고객 정보를 제대로 반영하는지 따진다.

An advisory commentary asks whether LLM investment advice truly uses the client profile.

Elisabetta Basilico, PhD, CFA

  • LLM은 그럴듯한 맞춤형 추천을 즉석에서 만든다
  • 유창함 뒤에 고객 정보 반영 여부가 숨는다
  • AI는 조언자를 보조할 뿐 수탁자가 아니다
방법
대규모 언어모델(LLM)의 투자 추천 생성 과정을 논평 형식으로 짚는다.
데이터
이론 연구
시사점
LLM 리서치 요약을 보조로만 쓰고 최종 배분 결정은 규칙과 사람이 맡는다.
적용도 1/5
매매 규칙이 없는 실무 논평이라 자동화할 대상이 없고, 검증할 데이터셋 자체를 제시하지 않는다.
  • LLMs produce polished, personalized-sounding recommendations instantly
  • Fluency hides whether the full client profile drives the output
  • AI assists advisors; it does not carry fiduciary duty
Method
Commentary on large language models generating client investment recommendations.
Data
Theory only
Use
Keep LLMs on research summarization; leave allocation decisions to explicit rules and humans.
Score 1/5
Score 1: a practitioner commentary with no signal, no rules, and no dataset to source or backtest.
large language modelsinvestment advicefiduciary dutyclient profilingadvisor automation
ORIGINAL ABSTRACTLarge language models can generate investment recommendations instantly. They can process client profiles, summarize market conditions, and produce polished rationales that sound personalized. But there is an important question underneath the fluency. Are these systems actually integrating the full client profile when they make decisions? AI should assist advisors, but AI is NOT a fiduciary was originally published at Alpha Architect . Please read the Alpha Architect disclosures at your convenience.
